approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
approach_variants.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. THERE IS NO BRIDGE OVER CANYON CREEK on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is UNSIGNED, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the SOUTH shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. FIRST, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. SECOND, at about 7,600 ft THE TRAIL ENDS — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. THIRD, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping RIBBON OF WHITE ROCK and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight UP that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line TRAVERSES ACROSS the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow ARROW, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE FINISHED THE HARD PART, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ENDS well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the WEST — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the HIGHEST summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile EAST. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

approach_variants.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it EXISTS TO AVOID THE CANYON CREEK FORD. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit end of the day is the same regardless of how you got into the basin: the trail dies around 7,600 ft into a loose gully marked by a ribbon of white rock and a yellow X, the paint leads you up rather than across, and the scrambling finishes well below the top where real trail resumes for the last quarter mile.

What differs is your bearing on arrival. Coming round by Devils Dome you meet the peak from the north-east rather than up from Crater Lake, so identify the south-ridge false top and the white ribbon from a distance before dropping into the basin, rather than expecting to walk into them off a known trail.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
approach_variants.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a long gravel road that is often still snowed shut into early or mid July, and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.
approach_variants.season: July to mid-August
hazards: Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's ice cliffs onto the traverse between camp and the bergschrund
Bare rock at the crux chimney in lean years, which raises both the grade and the rockfall
Bergschrund and crevasses at the start of the technical ground, around 9,800 ft
Sustained 45 to 60 degree snow and ice, with a long exposed rising traverse
Rockfall off decomposing volcanic cliffs on everything below about 12,200 ft
Overhanging rock step on the knife edge into high camp
Mowich Lake Road frequently closed by snow into July, and a descent that finishes at a different trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet BELOW it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately EAST of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly SOUTH above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops WEST off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back EAST, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

approach_variants.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon
approach_variants.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens well before Mowich Lake Road does, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May to early July
hazards: Hours of exposure to rockfall and icefall crossing beneath Willis Wall and the Liberty Wall
Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's cliffs onto the traverse into the route
Crevasses on the Winthrop and the Carbon, thin bridges early and open cracks late
Committing traverse with no quick exit once past Curtis Ridge
Sustained 45 to 60 degree ice and a rock or mixed crux around 12,000 ft
Very little traffic, so no established track above the Carbon and a slow rescue
Losing the faint Emmons descent to the well-trodden Disappointment Cleaver at the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: This is the approach on which Rainier's two Liberty Cap routes actually get confused, and the trap is a physical one: there is usually a bootpack running from St. Elmo Pass to the Carbon Glacier, and it was stamped in by parties going to LIBERTY Ridge. It is the right track as far as the Carbon and the wrong one after that. Working west you cross under Willis Wall and meet a narrow rock and snow ridge dropping straight to the glacier. That first spine is Liberty Ridge. Keep going. Past it the ground opens beneath a big pale cirque wall capped by hanging ice, and the next crest beyond that wall, roughly a mile and a half further west, is Ptarmigan Ridge. Put it the simple way and it is hard to get wrong: on Liberty Ridge the Liberty Wall is on your right, and on Ptarmigan Ridge it is on your left. Cross the Carbon below the seracs, gain the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge up to the flat high camp at 10,200 to 10,300 ft. That flat is the base of the climb, and four things fix it together: room for a couple of small tents, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon immediately east, banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and Liberty Ridge in full view straight across. From camp the route drops WEST off the crest onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, near a rock outcropping about the middle of the face — study that crossing from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there. Above the schrund the line rises back east, climber's left, toward the ice cliffs. If you have crossed a schrund with no ice cliff up and left of you, you are on the wrong part of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line at or just below the Terrible Traverse, and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It commits you to the Terrible Traverse rather than the Finger Traverse — the harder and more exposed of the two crossings
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM ON THIS ROUTE IS TELLING THIS CHUTE FROM THE OTHER ONE, AND THE TEST IS: KEEP WALKING UP THE CANYON PAST THE FIRST CHUTE. The published instruction for the South Chute is to start climbing east as soon as the CAT EARS tower is visible, and trip reports describing this line say plainly that you bypass the South Chute entrance and continue up loose talus to the MOUTH OF THE NORTH CHUTE further into Avalanche Canyon. So the discriminator is temporal, not visual: the first opportunity to leave the canyon eastward is the wrong one. IN CLOUD, where the Cat Ears cannot be seen at all, this is still workable because the test is about the canyon floor under your feet rather than about a skyline. From the lake, follow the canyon NORTH. Do not turn uphill at the first gully. Keep going on the talus until the canyon delivers you to a second, more northerly couloir, and take that. THE CONFIRMING TEST IS ABOVE THE CHUTE, and it is what proves you took the right one: the North Chute leads toward the Terrible Traverse, the steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff at roughly 7,435 ft. The South Chute leads to a notch at about 6,600 ft with the Cat Ears tower just left of it and then, after a saddle and a 150 ft descent and a second gully, to the Finger Traverse — a downsloping ledge with a horizontal finger crack and old pitons. If you top out and find a finger crack, you took the South Chute; if you top out and find a snow traverse over a cliff, you took this one. HONEST LIMIT: this chute is documented mostly as a variation inside other parties' loops. It is long, loose and less travelled, and there is no marker sequence inside the gully itself.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into UPPER Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ONE APPROACH WHERE THE NORTH CHUTE IS THE EASY ONE TO FIND, BECAUSE YOU ARRIVE ABOVE IT. Dropping into Avalanche Canyon from Crystal Pass on the intermittent climbers' path, the FIRST couloir that offers a line up onto the Constance side is the North Chute. Take it. If you keep descending the canyon you will next pass the Cat Ears and the Thumb and eventually reach the South Chute entrance and then the lake — every one of which means you have gone below the route.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE LAKE APPROACH: this chute delivers you toward the TERRIBLE TRAVERSE, a steep exposed snow crossing directly above a large cliff at roughly 7,435 ft, reached after the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges. If you top out on a notch with a tower just to its left and then find a saddle, a 150 ft drop and a ledge with a horizontal finger crack, you have found the South Chute and the Finger Traverse instead.

HONEST LIMIT: the climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass, so this variant's own approach is the navigationally hard part, not the chute.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road (standard)
approach_variants.notes:
Pull off at the old White Salmon lodge site on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate, and follow the old road past the lodge for about a mile to where it finishes in an old clearcut.

What you do next depends entirely on snow cover, and getting this wrong is the single biggest time sink on the approach. With GOOD cover, drop northeast off the clearcut down to White Salmon Creek and walk the valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — pleasant going. WITHOUT good cover, do not descend into the valley at all: hold your elevation as you enter the clearcut and contour around instead, giving up height only where a rock band or a stream crossing forces it. The valley bottom without snow is slide alder and devil's club.

From the glacier area, the route continues up toward the shoulder at the foot of the face.
approach_variants.season: spring to early summer; needs snow cover
hazards: avalanches off the Hanging Glacier, which is very active and sweeps the approach terrain
slide alder and devil's club in the White Salmon valley once the snow has gone
unbridged stream crossings when contouring the low-snow variation
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the shoulder at about 5,500 ft on the divide between the White Salmon Glacier and the Price cirque, and it is confirmed by what you can see BEHIND and BELOW you rather than above: from the shoulder you look down onto Price Lake. If Price Lake is not below you, you have not gained the shoulder — you are still on the glacier or on its moraine, and the face above you is foreshortened enough that it will look like the start.

The shoulder has good bivy sites, which is the second confirmation: flat ground here is scarce, so a usable bivy platform at this height on this ridge is the place.

From there the face itself is entered by a gully angling up and to the LEFT onto the North Face. Some parties instead continue up the glacier past the shoulder; if you have passed the bivy ground and are still on continuous glacier, you have gone by the entrance.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: An alternative used mainly by ski parties: start at the base of Chair 8 in the ski area and make a downhill traverse into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley, then climb over four thousand feet up the glacier. It removes the clearcut and the road walk at the cost of a long climb from the valley floor and a committing descent to start the day.
approach_variants.season: winter/spring, on skis
hazards: avalanche exposure from the Hanging Glacier across the whole basin
the initial descent commits you to regaining that height on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same shoulder at roughly 5,500 ft with Price Lake visible below to the north-west. Coming up from the valley floor rather than contouring in, the trap is stopping at the first flat ground on the glacier's margin — keep going until you are on the divide itself and the ground on the far side falls away toward Price Lake.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
approach_variants.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
hazards: the same ford, avalanche-debris zone and brushy climbers' path as the standard approach
a descent onto a large crevassed icefield with the return climb still to come
a long traverse beneath a face, exposed to anything coming off it
a bergschrund at the base of the face
a shaded north aspect that holds hard ice and cold, with a committing position
an approach that reaches its base by losing height, so retreat means re-climbing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEFINING INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU DO NOT TURN UPHILL AT THE COL THE STANDARD ROUTE USES. From the glacier col, descend onto the big icefield and KEEP TRAVERSING EAST BENEATH THE PEAK. The base of this route is out on that ice, under the face, not at any saddle.

IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED TO A COL WITH A BERGSCHRUND ON IT AND ARE LOOKING AT AN EASY SNOWFIELD CONTOURING ROUND TO A SUNNY SIDE, YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE STANDARD ROUTE'S ENTRY AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND GONE PAST YOUR OWN. Drop back onto the ice and continue east under the wall.

THE ASPECT IS THE OTHER TEST AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS. This face is the SHADED side. If the wall above you is in morning or afternoon sun while the icefield behind you is bright, you are round on the southern flank and looking at the wrong ground. The face should be holding shadow when the rest of the basin is not.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN, NOT JUST THE FACE. This summit sits just under a mile EAST of its larger and better-known neighbour along the connecting crest, and the same icefield runs beneath both. A north face reached quickly after crossing the first col is the neighbour's; keep traversing until the summit above you is the eastern one.

Watch the bergschrund at the foot of the face, which is a separate feature from the one on the standard route's col and behaves differently through the season.

approach_variants.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
approach_variants.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
hazards: long committed glacier travel with no camp of its own
crevasses across the whole traverse
exposure beneath a face for the length of the approach
a bergschrund at the foot of the wall
a plan that only makes sense inside a larger traverse, so a retreat is a multi-day proposition
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVING FROM THE WEST, THE ICEFIELD IS THE HIGHWAY AND THE PEAK IS PICKED OFF IT. Traverse east along the ice beneath the crest until the summit above you is the EASTERN of the two on this section of ridge - the larger, better-known peak lies just under a mile to the west, so the first big north face you pass is not yours.

THE FACE IS THE SHADED ONE. If the wall you are approaching takes direct sun while the ice around you is in shadow, you are on the wrong aspect or the wrong peak.

THE BASE IS ON THE ICE ITSELF, BENEATH THE WALL, with a bergschrund at the junction. THERE IS NO COL INVOLVED - if you have climbed to a saddle to reach your start, you have joined the standard route's entry on the far side of the crest instead.

Because this arrival involves no fixed camp of its own, fix a retreat plan before crossing beneath the face: the ground you traverse in to reach it is the ground you must reverse to leave, and it is all crevassed.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: The long way in from the west. Start at the Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road and work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor — Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek — on rugged, largely off-trail ground with real bushwhacking and glacier travel. Budget a full day, often two, before you are anywhere near rock. This is an experienced-mountaineers approach and nothing about it is a walk-in.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the bushwhacking is out of snow and the glaciers are travellable.
hazards: Open moat between glacier ice and the foot of the face; it hangs free enough that a rappel to the glacier has come off the rock well above the snow
Loose, poor-quality rock from the first pitch upward
Glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the approach and directly below the climb
Multi-day committing approach with no realistic quick exit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The east face of this peak rises directly out of the glacier, so the base of the climb is the ice-to-rock junction and the MOAT is the marker. Traverse the glacier under the east side until you find the point where the face rears up clean out of the ice rather than sitting back behind broken ground. The start is a finger-and-hand crack system you can step into straight out of the moat and follow for about a rope length to a ledge — if you cannot enter the crack from the moat without first scrambling talus, you are not at it. Expect the moat to be open and to need gear or a bridge; a recorded rappel back onto this glacier from above hung free over it, so the gap at the bottom is a permanent feature of this side rather than a bad year. Negative markers: if the wall in front of you is catching afternoon sun, you have crossed the crest and are on the WEST side of the peak; if you are looking up at a pair of clean dihedrals side by side, you are around on the ridge south of the summit at the start of the ridge route.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek from the east
approach_variants.notes: The other documented way into this range comes from the east, via the lake ferry and the long trail up Agnes Creek before leaving it for the brush. Parties using it camp on rock ridges above the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing on the same day. It is not a shortcut — the bushwhack off the trail takes most of a day on its own — but it puts you on the glacier side of the crest, which is the side this route starts from.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach with a full day of brush before any alpine ground
Crevasses and a persistent moat at the foot of the east faces
Loose rock throughout the climb
The peak is one of four closely spaced summits on one crest, easily confused from below
approach_variants.baseFinding: Camping on the ridges above the glacier puts you looking straight across at the east faces, which is the one view that makes this route findable: pick the line before you drop onto the ice, because from the glacier itself the faces foreshorten and the individual crack systems disappear. On the ice, work under the peak until the face rises clean from the moat and a finger-and-hand crack can be entered directly out of it. Negative marker: the peak is the southernmost of the four named summits on this short crest, so if you are still under a summit with more towers to the south of you, you are one peak too far north.

approach_variants.name: Up the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir to the C-J col
approach_variants.notes:
The East Ridge is reached from the Cascade-Johannesburg col, and the direct way there is to climb the couloir that names it. The start is the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft: walk back down the road, drop the embankment into the valley, cross the Cascade River, and go over the moraine onto the couloir apron at roughly 3,300 ft — about twenty minutes from leaving the road. Then roughly 3,000 ft of booting to the col.

This is the fast way and the dangerous way. The couloir carries rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier above, and the snow goes discontinuous where it narrows as the season progresses, so it is an early-season proposition.

The East Ridge by way of the C-J Couloir was first climbed in 1938 and is the most-used line on the peak; it and the other routes finishing on the south side are mostly scrambling.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun for continuous snow in the couloir
hazards: Rock and ice fall from the Sill hanging glacier in the couloir
Discontinuous couloir snow after early season
Loose rock and complicated route-finding on the ridge above the col
Existing rappel stations of unknown quality
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the Cascade-Johannesburg col itself — the notch at the top of the couloir, with Johannesburg on one side and Cascade Peak on the other. There is no ambiguity about arriving: the snow ends against the saddle and the ground drops away on the far side.

From the col the East Ridge is the crest running west toward Cascade Peak's summit, on your right as you top out of the couloir. Published descriptions of the ground above are thin and consistent on one point only: route-finding is complicated, exposure is significant, and loose rock is everywhere. Parties commonly climb it unroped while carrying a harness in case they want a belay.

There are numerous rappel stations scattered around this area from previous parties, and reports note that some of them need improving before use — treat a found anchor as information, not as confirmation you are on route.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The walking way in, avoiding the couloir entirely. Follow the Cascade Pass Trail from the trailhead at 3,600 ft for 3.5-3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at roughly 5,400 ft. At the pass, near the benches, turn right and pick up the obvious climbers' path onto Mixup Arm.

Cross Mixup Arm and traverse and descend rightward until you reach the Cache Glacier — the described landmark is a seasonal waterfall, past which you turn right and ascend the lobe of the Cache.

One party using this side reported a long sidehill traverse beneath the Triplets and Cascade Peak, camping in a meadow below the C-J col at about 6,200 ft. That camp puts you at the base of the East Ridge for the following morning without ever entering the couloir.

Early season the traverse across Mixup's flank is snow-covered with a poor runout; late season Cache Col and the glacier edges can moat out.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Snow-covered traverse on Mixup's flank with bad runout in early season
Cache Col and glacier margins moat out late season
Steep short snow tongue and flanking bergschrunds at Gunsight Notch
Rockfall in the confined ground between snow and rock at the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Approaching from this side you arrive at the C-J col or the meadows just below it rather than climbing up to it, so the confirmation is positional: the col is the saddle between Johannesburg and Cascade Peak at the head of the couloir, and from the meadow camp below it the East Ridge runs up on the Cascade Peak side.

Gunsight Notch — the prominent notch to the west of Cache Col — is the published portal from the Cache Glacier side for Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, so a party approaching Cascade Peak from the Cache rather than from the col is aiming at that notch instead. The snow tongue to Gunsight Notch is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees, with bergschrunds on either side of it dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and rockfall in tight quarters between snow and rock.

approach_variants.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile SHORT of Chikamin Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the 5,200 ft pack camp and make it a two or three day trip.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: An unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — overshooting puts you in the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
A steep, snow-filled and rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed class 3 moves on the summit horn
A long trail approach with camps well short of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS TO LEAVE THE TRAIL BEFORE YOU REACH THE PASS, AND THAT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE ENOUGH THAT IT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. At roughly mile 13.5 — about HALF A MILE SHORT of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp at about 5,200 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

THE NEGATIVE IS EXPLICIT AND EXPENSIVE: do NOT continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the FOUR BROTHERS, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

SO USE THE PACK CAMP AS THE MARKER: an established camp at about 5,200 ft on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO, IN ORDER: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 CHIMNEY or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

SNOW CHANGES THE CHARACTER OF THE GULLY ENTIRELY: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies
Exposure near the final ridge crest
Snow-filled gullies in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THIS SIDE THE ARRIVAL IS A LAKE, NOT A TRAIL JUNCTION: you climb the gullies directly ABOVE GLACIER LAKE. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

WHAT THE GROUND BELOW THE GULLIES LOOKS LIKE, AS CONFIRMATION: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

THE TWO APPROACHES MEET ON THE SAME UPPER MOUNTAIN, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE APPLIES ONCE YOU ARE ON THE PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.

approach_variants.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake OUTLET, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges can be slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
The outlet crossing below the dam is a real crossing, not a step-across
Cirque talus is loose and the boulder-hop to the wall is ankle-breaking ground
Snow can linger in the approach terrain into early summer
No water above Colchuck Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are looking for the START OF THE WEST FACE ROUTE on a wall that carries half a dozen hard lines, so the useful information is what sits either side of it.

The West Face route's first pitch begins at a LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the base of the wall. That corner is the thing to find. From the talus you scramble up to a ledge and the first pitch goes from there.

Orient yourself with the neighbours: The Tempest starts LOWER than the West Face and lies to its RIGHT, taking a system of cracks up a black-streaked headwall — the black streaking is visible from the talus and is a good negative marker. The Scoop is further RIGHT again, right of both the West Face and the Tempest. Scarface climbs the large, obvious pale rock SCAR on the formation, several hundred feet right of the old northwest buttress line. If you are under black streaks or under a conspicuous scar, you are right of where you want to be.

Rack up on the talus rather than at the wall — the base is boulders and the flat ground is below.

approach_variants.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the LEFTMOST gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
hazards: Slide alder band is a real bushwhack; cairns are the only guide
1,000 ft of loose gully
Lingering snow in the gully into early summer
More elevation gain than the outlet approach
No water above Colchuck Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Once you contour east into the cirque, the base identification is the same as the outlet approach: find the LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the foot of the wall, and use the black-streaked headwall of The Tempest and the pale rock scar of Scarface, both to the RIGHT, to confirm you have not drifted along the base.

The difference this way in is that you arrive in the cirque from the south, higher up, so your first sight of the wall is from the side rather than head-on. Walk out into the talus and look at the face square-on before committing to a start; foreshortened from the flank, several corners look like the corner.

approach_variants.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: a rooty, eroded and very slick steep mile that is worse descending than ascending
an easy-to-miss junction at the saddle where the two routes on this peak diverge
no water on the steep climb from the roadbed
rolling ridge travel that takes longer than the distance suggests
an exposed camp and no bail-out once out on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE JUNCTION AT THE SADDLE IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS APPROACH AND IT IS EASY TO MISS. At the ridge saddle near Point 5116, GO LEFT and climb about a thousand feet to Peak 5791. IF YOU FIND YOURSELF DROPPING TOWARD A LAKE, OR CONTOURING THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST ON A FAINT TREAD, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE OTHER BRANCH AND ARE ON THE KINDY RIDGE LINE THAT SERVES THE STANDARD ROUTE.

THE PINK RIBBON IS THE HANDRAIL ON THE STEEP MILE BELOW. It is spaced closely enough that losing sight of it for long means you have drifted; the tread is rooty and eroded and very slick when wet, so on the descent the ribbon matters more than the ground does.

ABOVE THE SADDLE THE MARKERS ARE TWO NAMED HIGH POINTS IN ORDER: Peak 5791 first, then heather benches and meadows above the lake, then Peak 5860 crossed or contoured. YOU SHOULD PASS TWO DISTINCT POINTS BEFORE THE RIDGE BEGINS - arriving at what you take for the base without having crossed them means you are short.

THE BASE ITSELF IS WHERE THE EAST RIDGE RISES OUT OF THE GROUND ABOVE THE LAKE BASIN AND RUNS WEST TOWARD THE SUMMIT. IF THE GROUND AHEAD OF YOU IS A GLACIER RATHER THAN A RIDGE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED PAST THE RIDGE'S FOOT AND JOINED THE STANDARD ROUTE'S APPROACH TO THE ICE. The east ridge is rock and heather with air on both sides; the standard route crosses snow.

Note that the two routes on this peak describe the ridge junctions differently and one says go left where the other says stay right at a fork. They are not the same fork. Follow the description belonging to the route you intend to climb and use the physical markers - a ribbon-marked steep mile, a saddle, then two high points - rather than reconciling the two.

approach_variants.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Same window
hazards: no water above the lake
a wind-exposed basin camp
loose blocks where the ridge rises out of the benches
committing ridge travel with no easy descent off either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE BASE OF THE EAST RIDGE IS GAINED BY CROSSING OR CONTOURING PEAK 5860 AND CONTINUING ON HEATHER BENCHES ABOVE THE BASIN. The ridge foot is where that benched ground runs out against the crest and the rock begins rising west toward the summit.

THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE ON A CREST, NOT ON A BENCH. Once established the ground should fall away on both sides. Heather benches with a wall above you and the basin below are still the approach.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS SNOW. IF YOU ARE STEPPING ONTO GLACIER ICE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED ROUND PAST THE FOOT OF THE RIDGE AND ARE ON THE STANDARD ROUTE'S GROUND. Turn back and gain the crest.

Carry water from the lake. There is none on the ridge.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (the historic standard)
approach_variants.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak and the road access has been unreliable for a very long time. The last several miles of FR 23 to the White Chuck trailhead have been reported blocked — at one point with large boulders placed at the turnoff — and reports of the road being driveable and undriveable have alternated over the years. Confirm with the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie forest before relying on it, because in a bad year the effective trailhead moves miles downstream.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: unreliable road access to the trailhead over many years
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes STRAIGHT UP the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk and the PCT (the reliable alternative)
approach_variants.notes: Because the White Chuck side has been unreliable for years, parties reach this side of the mountain instead from the North Fork Sauk River trailhead, climbing to White Pass on the PCT and then travelling north over Red Pass toward the Glacier Creek and Sitkum ground. It is substantially longer and is chosen for access rather than for the climbing.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Arriving from the north on the PCT the risk is passing the drainage entirely, so identify the Sitkum Creek and Glacier Creek junctions on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail to Pass No Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the highway junction take the state route north, then the loop road and the Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) to its end at the Trinity trailhead. Check current road status before committing to the drive: the road has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, which cuts off drive-in access entirely. From the trailhead hike the Buck Creek trail, climbing steadily through forest and along the creek to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off to the right. This is normally done as part of a backpacking trip to the pass rather than in a day, and the peak sits about half a mile northeast of that pass on the crest.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the high meadows melt out. The alternative grass-and-heather line is likely hazardous when wet.
hazards: A false trail lies just before the real cutoff, and on the way down the fork that crosses the creek into the woods is the wrong one
Road access to the trailhead has been closed below it at times, and fire closures have shut the trail — confirm before driving in
The boot path braids into several strands above about 5,800 ft
Exposed meadow crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
A short scramble on the block itself, easy rock but genuinely a scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CUTOFF IS AFTER THE MAIN STREAM, AND THERE IS A FALSE TRAIL BEFORE IT. Well up the Buck Creek trail you cross a series of streams; the turn to the right for Pass No Pass comes after the main one, is unmarked, and is quite obvious once you are at it — but a false trail branches before that crossing and is the thing parties take by mistake. Coming back down, the fork that crosses the creek and heads into the woods is the false one; go left instead. A single established campsite sits just above the first stream and is a useful confirmation. From the turn a path runs north to a bare patch, then a fainter track aims north-northwest toward a grey stone block just above the edge of the trees, which gives the bearing. Above about 5,800 ft the path splits repeatedly — ignore the spurs, keep going uphill and north, and the strands consolidate at Pass No Pass, a saddle near 6,380 ft in a grove of mature conifers. At the pass or just short of it, make a sharp left and traverse uphill to the southwest; the summit block comes plainly into view as you gain height. Take it by the easy rock on its south, left-hand side, and do not settle for the false south summit standing beside it.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes
approach_variants.notes: The alternative stays on the trail past the off-trail turn and continues all the way to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes from the pass to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble to the top. It is the option for a party already camped at the pass on a backpacking trip, and it trades the braided boot path and the meadow traverse for a steeper direct climb.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn on dry ground only — this line is likely hazardous when the grass and heather are wet.
hazards: Steep grass and heather with poor runout, and likely hazardous when wet
No path on the climb from the pass
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
The same short scramble on the block itself
Exposed to afternoon weather with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding: YOU IDENTIFY THIS LINE BY STAYING ON THE TRAIL PAST THE TURN. Where the off-trail path breaks right toward Pass No Pass around 5,600 ft, ignore it and carry on along the maintained tread to Buck Creek Pass itself. From the pass the peak stands about half a mile to the northeast on the crest, and the slopes rising toward it are steep grass and heather rather than the meadowy braided path of the other line. Climb them to reach the west side of the summit block. The test that you are on this variant and not the other is underfoot: continuous steep vegetation with no worn path, approached from the pass rather than traversed into from the southwest. Do not commit to it when the grass is wet, because that surface gives no purchase and the slope runs out badly. Whichever side you arrive on, the block itself is taken by the easy rock on its south side; the steeper aspects are not the route.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
approach_variants.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb west to north-west, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
approach_variants.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TIMBER BELT IS THE NAVIGATION, THE GLACIER TOE IS THE ARRIVAL. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

THE CAMP IS A FLAT BENCH, NOT A VIEWPOINT. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench directly below the toe of the ice. If you are on sloping heather with the ice still out of sight above you, keep going; if you are already on the ice you have walked past the bench.

THE HEADWALL IS ABOVE THE GLACIER, NOT AT ITS TOE. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. IF YOU ARE ROPING UP AND SWINGING TOOLS WITHIN MINUTES OF LEAVING CAMP, YOU ARE ON A SERAC OR A CREVASSE WALL LOW ON THE GLACIER, NOT ON THE HEADWALL. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A CROSS-CHECK AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
approach_variants.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LANDING THE FIRST TASK IS TO GET ONTO THE TRAIL AND FIND MAY CREEK - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

THE ONE THING THE BOAT CHANGES IS YOUR MARGIN, NOT YOUR ROUTE. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.

approach_variants.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
approach_variants.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
approach_variants.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROAD SECTION IS NAVIGATION-FREE; THE APPROACH STILL STARTS AT MAY CREEK. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

WHAT CHANGES IS WHERE THE SNOW STARTS. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. IF THE PASSAGE YOU WOULD NORMALLY TAKE THROUGH A BAND IS A SMOOTH, WIND-LOADED RAMP RATHER THAN A BOOT TRACK, TREAT IT AS AVALANCHE TERRAIN AND NOT AS A ROUTE.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case the arrival marker is the change of angle where the ground stops climbing and the ice begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the LAST RELIABLE WATER; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet BELOW the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
Loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final scramble to the wall
Loose basin talus
Long dry stretch above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Let It Burn starts in the base gully on the wall's lower-LEFT section, and the last move of the approach is a scramble up a THIRD-CLASS RAMP out of the gully to the foot of the technical climbing. Ramp, not gully floor — belaying from the gully bed means you are below the start. A documented party took about three hours and 47 minutes from trailhead to base, which matches the three-and-a-half to four hour figure the route carries; substantially longer usually means the alder band or the wrong gully.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-LEFT off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band — a real bushwhack
Loose gully talus; snow lingering in the gully into early summer
Cairns stop at the base of the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are a couple of cairns at the BASE of the correct gully and none above it, so do not expect to be led up. Leftmost is the discriminator: a gully further right will not top out into the basin. From the basin, Let It Burn starts on the wall's lower-left section, and the technical climbing begins above a third-class ramp out of the base gully rather than at the gully floor.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
approach_variants.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
approach_variants.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GAP. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an OPEN BENCH, and above the bench you cross a SNOWFIELD into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's LEFT for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
approach_variants.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's NORTHEAST BASIN. The route is guarded by a RIDGE NOTCH, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a LARGE VERTICAL CRACK forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
From the Dosewallips River Road washout at roughly 700 ft, about 5 miles of road-walk or bike on the closed road, crossing Constance Creek on wooden footbridges near the start, to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft.

The trail gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — one of the steepest approaches in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutal and eases only slightly into denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps needing hands. Expect scramble-grade tread with no switchbacks and cairn-and-flagging route-finding in places. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a full pack. Water at Constance Creek partway and at the lake outlet; treat everything.

The trail skirts the lake's east shore to established campsites at the north end, in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Most parties camp there rather than going car to car. From camp, head north up scree into the canyon's lower basin, then bend east along a rib.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Residual snow in the South Chute makes it a far better climb than bare scree does
hazards: The Finger Traverse is a highly exposed, downsloping narrow ledge; footholds are marginal even with the crack in hand
Reversing it on descent goes round a blind corner and most parties find that harder than the way up
1,900 ft of loose scree in the South Chute, which sluffs rock onto parties below
The fixed pitons on the traverse are decades old — do not trust them without inspection
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; the descent takes many parties nearly as long as the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS A TOWER CALLED THE CAT EARS, AND THE PUBLISHED INSTRUCTION IS A TRIGGER RATHER THAN A DESCRIPTION: BEGIN CLIMBING THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS ARE VISIBLE. Follow Avalanche Canyon north from the lake — roughly 0.6 mile — and watch east. The Cat Ears is the tower standing just LEFT of the notch you are aiming for at the top of the chute. The moment it comes into view, turn east and start up. Starting later means more scree; starting earlier puts you on the wrong ground.

IN CLOUD, WHEN THE CAT EARS CANNOT BE SEEN, THE FALLBACK IS THE CHUTE'S OWN SHAPE. The South Chute is a long gully that NARROWS as it climbs, gaining about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft at the notch in the south ridge. It is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake. If the gully you are in is widening rather than narrowing, or if you are still walking north up the canyon bed after well over half a mile, you have passed it and are heading for the North Chute and the Terrible Traverse instead.

SECOND TEST, and it is what confirms you were right about the chute: above the notch you cross a saddle, DROP about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge. A route that only ever goes up is not this one — the deliberate loss of height above the first notch is part of the line. From there the route threads gaps and ledges marked in places by faded WHITE PAINT DOTS. Painted dots are man-made, they do not move, and they are visible at arm's length in fog; if you are seeing them you are on the line.

THE FINGER TRAVERSE ITSELF IS A TACTILE TEST, WHICH IS THE BEST KIND HERE: a downsloping ledge above a large cliff with a HORIZONTAL CRACK running along its top edge, which you jam your fingers into for balance because the footholds are thin. A rusty decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along it. If there is no continuous crack at hand height above the ledge you are standing on, that is not the Finger Traverse.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail entirely. From the Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end. Take the Constance Pass Trail up through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft, then leave the trail and go cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and up to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass descend south into Avalanche Canyon on an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the north side of the canyon, and continue DOWN the canyon toward the lake until the South Chute opens on your left (east).

This is considerably longer than the lake approach and it exists because the lake trail is brutally steep, unmaintained and blowdown-choked. Most parties on it are on a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country travel between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass, on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass beyond transient snowmelt
Every hazard on the Finger Traverse itself, reached at the end of a longer day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ENTERING THE CANYON FROM CRYSTAL PASS PUTS THE CAT EARS TEST THE OTHER WAY UP: you must descend PAST the North Chute before the South Chute opens. The Cat Ears tower and the formation trip reports call the Thumb both sit in this stretch of canyon, and on this side you pass them going down rather than meeting them going up.

THE RELIABLE TEST ON THIS SIDE IS THE CHUTE'S TOP, NOT ITS BOTTOM. The South Chute tops out at a notch in the SOUTH ridge at roughly 6,600 ft, with the Cat Ears tower standing just left of that notch. Coming down the canyon from Crystal Pass you can pick your entry by which notch the gully above you leads to: the one with a tower just left of it is the South Chute. The chute that leads straight toward the Terrible Traverse without a tower beside its notch is the North Chute.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the lake approach and they are the good ones: cross the saddle, LOSE about 150 ft, up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge, then gaps and ledges marked with faded WHITE PAINT DOTS, then a downsloping ledge with a continuous horizontal finger crack along its top edge and old fixed pitons in it.

HONEST LIMIT: the track fades near Crystal Pass and the drop into the canyon is unmarked. This variant is longer and navigationally harder; it is chosen for the trail it avoids, not for the ground it crosses.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; STAY LEFT at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the UPHILL fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE COL BETWEEN FRICABA AND HAL FOSS, AND THE PUBLISHED TEST FOR IT IS THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS PEAK THAT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: FROM DECEPTION BASIN, ASCEND EASTWARD AIMING FOR THE LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS. Lowest point. Not the nearest gully, not the most obvious scree fan — the lowest saddle on that connecting ridge. In cloud you can still tell which way a skyline sags by walking toward the direction the ground stops climbing soonest.
