SECOND TEST, once at the col: turn AWAY from Hal Foss and follow the ridge up to Fricaba. The North and SW ridges are the two most readily ascended and this is the SW one. The first 500 to 600 vertical feet off the pass is the STEEPEST part of the climb; after that it eases into a straightforward scree hike. So the shape of the effort is a check on the line: steep first, easy after. A route that stays uniformly moderate is not this one.

THIRD TEST, AND IT IS WHICH SUMMIT: FRICABA'S SW PEAK IS THE TRUE, HIGHER TOP. The NE peak lies about half a mile away along the NE ridge and is noticeably lower. If you have walked half a mile of ridge from the top you reached and are now standing somewhere higher, you were on the NE peak.

WHAT THE GROUND FEELS LIKE, so it does not read as a wrong turn: Fricaba is extremely shattered, rotten shale. Two steps up and one slide back is the normal experience, not evidence you are off route. Brief Class 2-3 scrambling appears near the ridge crest.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the LEFT of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: SAME BASE, SAME TEST, APPROACHED ACROSS THE BASIN RATHER THAN DOWN INTO IT: from Deception Basin, ascend EASTWARD aiming for the LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS. THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is the gendarmes on the way up: the usual line goes round them to the LEFT, then up steep scree. If you are scrambling over towers rather than skirting them, you have taken the crest instead of the scree. AND THE SAME SUMMIT TEST: THE SW PEAK IS THE TRUE TOP. The NE peak, half a mile off along the NE ridge, is lower. HONEST LIMIT: the scree route above the col is considered self-explanatory, which means there is no known marker for it. It is a walk-up on rubbish rock; the navigation problem is getting to the col, not what happens above it.

approach_variants.name: Mount Pilchuck Road to the trailhead
approach_variants.notes: From Granite Falls take the highway east and then the Mountain Loop about ten or eleven miles to the ranger station. Continue about a mile past it, cross the river, and turn south onto the Mount Pilchuck road. Follow it roughly seven miles — a mix of paved and rough washboarded gravel that varies year to year with maintenance — to the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet.
approach_variants.season: July to October. The trail is typically snow-covered into early or midsummer in some years, and traction is commonly needed through June.
hazards: Fatal falls have occurred on the exposed final scramble and lookout rocks, particularly in wet or icy conditions
Search and rescue is called to this peak several times a season, mostly for lost or injured parties on the boulder field and the old ski-slope ground
Snow obscures the trail and the painted boulder-field markers into early summer
The fixed ladder's rungs can spin underfoot
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts where the forest tread runs out at the OPEN TALUS AND BOULDER FIELD below the summit headwall, and the marker there is paint, not tread: the route across the boulders is carried by ORANGE BLAZES PAINTED ON THE ROCKS. If you are following blazes on boulders rather than a footpath, you are on route; if you are following a footpath, you have not reached the boulder field yet. The finish is unmistakable — twenty to thirty feet of hands-on boulder scrambling to a short FIXED STEEL LADDER whose rungs can spin underfoot, leading onto the lookout deck. Negative markers: if you find yourself descending an open brushy clearing to the WEST of the trail, you have wandered onto the old ski-area slope, which looks like a shortcut and has contributed to lost-hiker rescues; and if you are following a creek up a gulch from a small lake with no blazes anywhere, you are on the peak's other route, which comes from a completely different trailhead on the far side.

approach_variants.name: From the Heather Lake trailhead when the road is gated
approach_variants.notes: In years when the road is gated below the trailhead, the walk starts from the Heather Lake trailhead instead, adding roughly five miles and substantial gain each way. Everything above the normal trailhead is identical, so this is a road-walk variant rather than a different climb, but it changes a half-day into a long one and is worth confirming before driving out.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder season, when the forest road is closed below the trailhead — common in spring and autumn.
hazards: A much longer day than the standard start, with the same exposed finish at the end of it
Same fall and route-finding hazards on the boulder field and summit rocks
Snow more likely on the upper mountain in the shoulder seasons when this variant applies
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same starting point as the standard approach — the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet — and from there the base of the scrambling is the same: the open talus and boulder field below the summit headwall, marked by ORANGE BLAZES PAINTED ON THE BOULDERS rather than by tread. The finish is the short fixed steel ladder onto the lookout deck. Negative marker: if you are still on road grade rather than trail, you have not reached the trailhead yet; the boulder field is well above it.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
approach_variants.notes: Get the free backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley east of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the hanging glacier itself, which is described as very active
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
A traverse with no easy retreat once committed, and a bivy on the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PRICE LAKE MUST STAY BELOW YOU AND TO YOUR WEST, AND THAT IS THE TEST. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's LEFT, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

ARRIVAL: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the SHOULDER — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

THE ERROR THAT KILLS PEOPLE HERE IS DRIFTING LEFT, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay RIGHT during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

AFTER 500 FT OF TRAVERSE the line goes UP, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Lower Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
hazards: A 1,000 ft descent that must be re-climbed on the return if you reverse this variant
Winnie's Slide, which is sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Committing to a route whose descent normally exits a different valley from the one you started in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE FROM ABOVE, SO THE TEST IS INVERTED — YOU ARE LOOKING FOR THE BOTTOM OF A DESCENT, NOT THE TOP OF A CLIMB. From the Lower Curtis bivy you drop roughly 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier. Stop descending when the ground lets you traverse northeast onto the northwest rib; if you keep going down the White Salmon you end up in the valley the other variant walked up, and you will have thrown away the whole approach.

THE RIB IS THE MARKER. The northwest rib is a defined feature between the White Salmon and the Hanging Glacier, and once you are on it the foot of the Hanging Glacier is the next thing you meet.

CONFIRM WITH THE SAME TEST THE OTHER VARIANT USES: from the base of the climbing, Price Lake should be below you and to the west, and you should be standing on the shoulder that separates the White Salmon cirque from the Price cirque, with a basin on each side of you.

AND THE SAME HARD RULE APPLIES: do not drift left onto the true North Face. It avalanches, and arriving from this side does not change that.

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
approach_variants.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin
crevasses on the glacier above the col
a wide gully that collects anything falling from the slopes above it
a high camp with a long committing retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL, NOT ON A FACE, AND THE COL IS BETWEEN TWO PEAKS. From the lake basin camp, gain the WIDE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF THE SADDLE and climb it to the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. The glacier route begins there.

RECOGNISE THE COL BY WHAT IS ON BOTH SIDES OF IT. You should be standing in a gap with a summit rising to either hand and ground falling away in front and behind. IF THE MOUNTAIN IS ABOVE YOU AND THERE IS NOTHING BEHIND YOU BUT THE SLOPE YOU CAME UP, YOU ARE ON A SHOULDER RATHER THAN THE COL.

THE GULLY IS THE POSITIVE MARKER ON THE WAY UP - a wide one, on the NORTH side of the saddle. A narrow gully, or one on the south side, is a different line.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER THAT MATTERS MOST: THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE ON THIS PEAK STARTS AT THE TOE OF A DIFFERENT GLACIER ON THE OTHER FLANK, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
approach_variants.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at the falls
an overgrown approach road that washes out
crevasses on the ice above the col
two routes leaving one camp, with the wrong turn costing a day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE DEPOT CREEK CAMP YOU ARE APPROACHING THE COL FROM THE OPPOSITE SIDE, so descriptions written from the other camp will have the gully and the col in the wrong relative positions - read the ground rather than the page.

THE FIXED POINT IS THE SAME: THE COL AT ABOUT 7,380 FT BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR TO THE NORTH-WEST. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully on the col's north side is the connection to the basin on the far side.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT GAP is that BOTH summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

DO NOT CONFUSE THIS START WITH THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. IF YOU HAVE NOT GAINED A COL, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail #813 to Lake of the Angels, then the rock rib above the basin
approach_variants.notes: this route and the Lake of the Angels route appear to be the same climb entered twice. The variants here are written for the ground the route itself describes. Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813) at about 1,565 ft on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25). A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles; check Forest Service status. The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek a few hundred feet, then starts a long unrelenting climbing traverse west, gaining nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles without easing. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an OLD LOGGING ROAD, and the tread is easy to lose there — look for the continuation slightly DOWNHILL. Around 4,200 ft comes the short headwall with an old hand-line or a large exposed tree root as the handhold, the crux of the trail and a common turnaround point when wet. Maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles at about 4,500 ft, and a rougher way-trail continues up steep rocky ground to Lake of the Angels at about 4,900 ft near 4 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Consolidated snow has been reported from about 4,500 ft up well into summer in the north-facing basin above the lake
hazards: Exposed scramble moves near the summit block and a 15-20 ft Class 4 crack step with no fixed anchor
Lingering steep snow in the north-facing basin above the lake into early-mid summer
Route-finding above Lake of the Angels is loose and nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow
The 4,200 ft headwall on the trail is greasy when wet and the hand-line is not maintained
The tread is easy to lose where it crosses the old logging road at about 1.3 miles
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CLIMB STARTS WHERE THE TRAIL ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A RIB, NOT A SUMMIT VIEW. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail: climb roughly 800 ft up onto the ROCK RIB above the lake's basin and CROSS TO ITS NORTH SIDE. A rib is a shape underfoot — the ground rises to a spine and falls away on both sides — so it is identifiable in cloud, and the instruction to cross to the far side of it is a check you can perform without seeing anything. SECOND TEST: from the north side of the rib, Class 2-3 terrain leads up toward a NOTCH ON MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, BELOW the feature called ST. PETER'S GATE. Below, not through. St. Peter's Gate is the notch in the SOUTHEAST ridge and it belongs to the traverse from Lena Lake; the notch you want is on the WEST ridge and sits lower and to the south of it. If you have walked up to a notch that opens onto an entirely different basin to the east, that is the Gate and you are past your turn. THIRD TEST, on the summit block: the final 150 to 200 ft is mostly Class 3 but contains one well-documented 15 to 20 ft CLASS 4 STEP up a SHALLOW CRACK, often marked by a CAIRN. A cairn is man-made and does not move. If you have reached the top without meeting a short crack step, you are on a sub-summit — this mountain has three, and parties confuse them in fog. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TIMING SAYS: Mountaineers reports for this line log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car to car. CAUTION FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is route-finding advice rather than a hazard note: at least one party took a steep mossy waterfall gully as a descent shortcut and found it far worse than reversing the ascent. Reverse the rib; do not improvise a line down the south side.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the St. Peter's traverse, arriving at the Gate from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The long way to the same mountain, kept here because it is a genuinely different approach rather than a variation of the Putvin walk. Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft and 6.5 miles. From there, off-trail west past Lena Tarn and Scout Lake to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake and round into Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above Ullin's Bathtubs, then a rising traverse to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending on loose moraine, and finally exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

Most parties then continue southwest about half a mile into the Lake of the Angels basin, which is where this approach rejoins the Putvin ground, and exit down the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake, so plan a shuttle or a stashed bike.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive off-trail route-finding across Scout Pass, Scout Basin and Ullin's Pass on faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt slopes below St. Peter's Gate
Requires a car shuttle or stashed bike between two trailheads about 4 road miles apart
Fog on the upper mountain, where parties have repeatedly lost the route
Unbridged stream crossings on the way-trail sections
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS ST. PETER'S GATE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT: the traverse's high point, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's SOUTHEAST ridge, reached up a steep snow-and-dirt ramp over loose moraine. Ground stops rising, notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens beyond. THE TEST THAT PUTS YOU ON THIS ROUTE'S LINE RATHER THAN THE GULLY LINE: from the Gate, continue southwest into the Lake of the Angels basin and pick the route up from there — the rock rib above the lake, crossed to its NORTH side, and Class 2-3 ground to the notch on the WEST ridge below the Gate. The alternative from the Gate is to drop about 300 ft directly to the base of a basalt cliff and take the south-face gully; that is the Lena Lake traverse route, a Class 3-4 gully, and a different climb. ABOVE THE WEST-RIDGE NOTCH THE TEST IS THE SAME: a short Class 4 step up a shallow crack, often cairned, in the last 150 to 200 ft, on a mountain with three summits. HONEST LIMIT: coming from the east adds a day and several passes of unmarked way-trail. It is chosen for the country, not for the climb.

approach_variants.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about a mile, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Self-issue Mt. Skokomish Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Aug. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus — spread the group out rather than stacking above and below
Sustained exposure on the Dog Walk Ledge / Catwalk, where the tread is one boot wide with drops on both sides
Steep avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring and early season
The scree field below the false summit is greasy and slick when wet
Significant elevation loss on descent, hard on knees and ankles, and slower than the climb
Route-finding through the forested lower section, meadows and talus in poor visibility
Little shade above treeline; the route gets hot
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE TERRAIN CHANGES AND EACH ONE IS A CHECK YOU CAN MAKE WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING. First: forest gives way to OPEN MEADOW BENCHES around 3,800 ft — that is where the ridgeline and neighbouring Mount Ellinor come into view on a clear day, and where the ground briefly eases. Second: above the meadows you enter SCREE AND TALUS and the rule is to stay primarily on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of a large loose rocky gully. Left side of the gully, all the way. Third: the path winds above the gully until it GAINS THE SOUTHERN RIDGELINE, and from there the ground drops away on BOTH sides.

THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR THE REAL CLIMBING IS THE SOUTH SADDLE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT, AND IT HAS TWO MARKERS: it is a KNOWN BIVY SITE, and it is the FIRST POINT ON THE ROUTE WHERE THE TRUE SUMMIT BECOMES VISIBLE. Flat ground you could sleep on, high on a ridge, is a thing you can identify by standing on it.

SECOND TEST, above the saddle: a STONE WIND SHELTER sits on the ridge. A built structure is unambiguous in any weather. From the wind shelter a final short Class 3-4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit. If you have topped out without passing a stone shelter, you are on the false summit below it.

THE SECTION IN BETWEEN IS THE ONE PEOPLE REMEMBER: the ridge-crest traverse called the Dog Walk Ledge or the Catwalk, where in several spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides. Class 3 with a couple of Class 3+/4 moves. If the crest you are on is comfortably wide the whole way, you have not reached it yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: a trip report warns specifically that contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Stay left of the drop-off on the north side.

approach_variants.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
approach_variants.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt on the connecting ridge with a crux gendarme downclimb of notably poor rock and severe exposure
Sustained Class 4 scrambling past gendarmes with a loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing terrain between two summits with no quick exit
All the Washington summit-ridge hazards at the end of it
approach_variants.baseFinding: COMING FROM ELLINOR THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR WASHINGTON'S SUMMIT GROUND IS THE SAME STONE WIND SHELTER on the ridge, with the final short Class 3-4 scramble above it to the 6,255 ft top. THE TEST ON THE CONNECTING RIDGE ITSELF, WHICH IS WHERE THE DAY IS DECIDED: hidden ledges keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below on most of the gendarmes, so if you are pulling harder than that you have taken the crest where a ledge existed. Look below the obvious line before committing to it. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, the usual answer is to DROP INTO THE BASIN BELOW and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger. HONEST LIMIT: the usual advice on the crux gendarme downclimb is to avoid it — the rock is notably poor and the exposure severe, and several parties recommend the west-side basin instead of the direct ridge. That is a recommendation to change route, not a marker, and this variant is written down mainly so a party knows the option exists before they are standing on it.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center (about 578 ft) the Hoh River Trail runs east up the valley for roughly 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at about 4,300 ft, past Five Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station and High Hoh Bridge near mile 9, Lewis Meadow near mile 11 (the usual overnight if you split the walk in), and Elk Lake near mile 15. A washed-out cliffside stretch around mile 16 is crossed on a fixed ladder; rungs have been reported missing in recent seasons, so look at it before you commit weight. Water is frequent the whole way.

From Glacier Meadows a way path climbs about 0.8 mile to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine and follows it roughly 0.2 mile before dropping onto the ice. That drop is loose and rockfall-prone; some parties fix a short line. Rope up on the ice. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading the rock islands to the right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to the crest of Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft. Snow Dome is the standard high camp, a thousand feet below the summit.

From Snow Dome the standard line goes up to and over Crystal Pass, then traverses just south of and below Five Fingers Ridge and over a false summit to the summit pyramid. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually bridged through midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier and the trail above Elk Lake is steep snow; later and the moat at the base of the summit rock opens and the ramps go from snow-covered to loose
hazards: Crevasses on the Blue Glacier and a large one near Crystal Pass, usually snow-bridged and not always
Rockfall on the moraine descent onto the ice, and a fixed-ladder washout around mile 16 of the trail
Loose rock on the east-face ramps and rockfall from parties above on them
A developing moat at the base of the summit rock in warm or late-season conditions, forcing a committing step onto rock
Whiteout on Snow Dome — the crevassed plateau is where the 1993 fatal unroped fall happened
A 17-mile walk out with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A FLAT TOP AT THE FOOT OF AN 80 FT TOWER, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT IS UNDERFOOT, NOT ON THE HORIZON. Off the false summit you drop into a sharp saddle, then climb a short steep snow slope with a clean runout. That slope ENDS FLAT. The moment the ground stops rising and you are standing on a small flat platform of snow with an 80 ft rock tower directly above you, you are at the base of the summit block, on its NORTHEAST side. There is nothing else on this mountain that is a flat snow top under an 80 ft tower. SECOND TEST, and it is the one that separates this finish from the two other routes on this same block: from that platform the East Face Ramps line goes RIGHT, around the corner onto the east face, and climbs a series of ramps angling up and across it before joining the last Class 4 / 5.4 step. If you are climbing straight up the face directly above the platform you are on the North Face Direct, and if you have walked round to the far side you are on the Northwest Edge. All three finish on the same 80 ft tower and all three start from this platform; the only thing that tells them apart is which way you turn. WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you are still gaining height on snow with no rock tower over you, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and have not yet dropped into the saddle. If you can see the Blue Glacier below you on your right the whole way, you are still on the traverse and have not reached Crystal Pass. HONEST LIMIT: the ramps themselves are loose and the correct one is chosen by eye. A fog test can get you to the foot of the block; it cannot pick the ramp for you.

approach_variants.name: From the Bailey Range: Queets Basin, Blizzard Pass and the Humes Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach of parties already on the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a way anyone drives to. It comes at Olympus from the SOUTH instead of the north: from the High Divide out of Sol Duc, along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, then down into Queets Basin, and up over Blizzard Pass onto the Humes Glacier. From the Humes the summit massif is gained from the south side and the summit block is reached from the opposite direction to the Snow Dome line.

It is longer by days and it exists in the record because traverse parties use it, not because it is easier. A party carrying glacier gear can also run it the other way and exit down the Blue Glacier to the Hoh, which is how most traverses finish.

Nothing about the approach shortens the climb: the last five hundred feet, the false summit, the saddle and the summit block are the same ground the Hoh parties cross.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Bailey Range crest is walkable and the Humes is not avalanching
hazards: Multi-day committing wilderness travel with no bail options once on the Bailey crest
Crevasses and icefall on the Humes Glacier
Blizzard Pass holds steep snow and is named for what happens there
Route-finding on the Bailey crest in cloud, where the ridge is the only handrail
No resupply and no reliable rescue access; NPS has reported multiple helicopter rescues per season among permitted Bailey parties
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME FLAT SNOW TOP UNDER THE 80 FT TOWER — the block does not care which side of the mountain you walked in from. What changes coming from the south is which way you meet the false summit: from the Humes side you are working up toward the summit ridge from below rather than dropping onto it from Crystal Pass, so the sharp saddle between the false summit and the true one is reached from the opposite end.

The test that you have not overshot on this side is Five Fingers Ridge. The standard line runs just SOUTH of and BELOW it. If Five Fingers Ridge is below you rather than above you, you are on the crest itself and too high; drop back under it and keep the ridge on your uphill side until the false summit is passed and the saddle opens.

HONEST LIMIT: this approach is thinly documented as an approach — it is described in traverse accounts, which are about the traverse. Treat the Hoh variant as the one with detail and this one as the one that gets a traverse party to the same platform.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
approach_variants.hours: 4-5 to camp, about 2 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes: Cascade River Road runs about 22-23 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead, a large lot at road's end at 3,600 ft. This is the only approach on this list that is on maintained trail almost the whole way. The Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks up through old-growth timber — roughly 35 switchbacks, about 1,800 ft in the first two miles — then eases through meadows to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft, 3.5-3.7 miles in. At the pass take the left (north) fork for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open ridge crest, about another 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft, to Sahale Glacier Camp at roughly 7,200-7,600 ft — rock-walled tent pads on the moraine, and the NPS-permitted high camp. Water is reliable at the creek crossings low on the trail, at Doubtful Lake (a signed spur, about a mile and 1,000 ft down and back) and from snowmelt near Sahale Glacier Camp early and mid season. Sources dry up late summer, so fill before the long switchback climb. Above camp the Sahale Glacier is small and low-angle by North Cascades standards but should still be treated as a glacier — rope up rather than assuming it out. Overnight camping is quota-limited and needs a North Cascades backcountry permit picked up in person at Marblemount.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock on the summit block, with parties directly above and below on a popular route
Exposed class 3-4 scrambling — many parties belay the last section
Meltwater runnels on the glacier disguising real crevasses late season
Water sources dry by late summer between the trailhead and Doubtful Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing is the summit pyramid above the glacier, and the mistake to avoid is attacking it straight on.

From the top of the glacier you arrive under the southwest side of the summit block. Do not start up the steepest ground directly in front of you. Trend right toward the notch, then onto the north/east side of the block — the correct line corkscrews around the peak rather than going up it. You should find yourself on a system of solid but increasingly exposed class 3 ledges, not on a face.

The last confirmation is a short class 4 move — about twenty feet of it, one awkward crack or chimney-like exit that puts you through a notch in the summit rocks onto the top. There is a fixed rappel station at that spot, and finding a fixed anchor is the clearest proof from the ground that you are on the standard line and not a variation.

The trap is the dihedral. Left of the standard notch there is a steeper dihedral feature that reads as the obvious line; it goes at fourth to low fifth class on loose rock and wants gear. If you are looking at a clean-cut corner rather than a rubble ledge that leads around and right, you are on the harder variation.

In poor visibility: the block is small and unmistakable once you are at it, so the navigation problem is the glacier, not the rock. Late season the glacier surface is cut by meltwater runnels that look like crevasses and crevasses that look like runnels — parties report going up and climber's right, climbing diagonally across the gullies, because that side reads more reliably.

approach_variants.name: Car-to-car day push
approach_variants.notes:
Because the approach is on maintained trail to about 7,200 ft, Sahale is regularly done in a single long day from the trailhead, which sidesteps the quota-limited high camp entirely. The trade is that you carry glacier gear the whole 6 miles up and 6 miles down, and you meet the summit block later in the day when it is busiest and the snow is softest.

Nothing about the line changes; only the logistics do. If the permit lottery has closed you out of Sahale Glacier Camp, this is the fallback rather than a different route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, long daylight
hazards: Long day with glacier gear carried the full distance
Arriving at the summit block in the afternoon queue
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical to the camp version — the pyramid above the top of the Sahale Glacier, gained by trending right to the notch and following ledges around the block to the short class 4 exit at the fixed rappel station.

approach_variants.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,050 to 5,800 ft depending on which record you read.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
hazards: an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass with no signage
a long enough round trip that many parties camp, so a day attempt commits to a late finish
loose rock on the tower and on the ridge approach to it
a two-pitch face that still needs a rope, a rack and a plan to get back down
no water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE PASS IS THE GATE AND THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES DIRECTLY FROM THE TOP OF IT. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs SOUTH along the ridge from the pass itself. IF YOU ARE CASTING ABOUT ON THE TRAIL BELOW THE PASS FOR A JUNCTION, YOU HAVE NOT GOT HIGH ENOUGH.

THE TOWER IS A DISTINCT ROCK TOWER ON THAT CREST AND IT IS THE FIRST ONE. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the NORTH-EAST side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOUNTAIN FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, YOU HAVE CONTINUED TO THE MOUNTAIN AND GONE PAST THE TOWER. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

THE ROUTE CONFIRMS ITSELF ON THE SECOND PITCH: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one DIAGONALLING LEFT INTO A GULLY AND FINISHING AT A LARGE BOULDER NEAR THE TOP. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.

approach_variants.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: more climbing than the other trailhead for a slightly shorter distance
forested trail the whole way, with little view of conditions ahead
an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass
loose rock on the tower
no water on the ridge beyond the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE APPROACH IS IDENTICAL TO THE OTHER TRAILHEAD'S: AN UNMAINTAINED CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES THE TOP OF THE PASS AND RUNS SOUTH ALONG THE RIDGE.

THE TOWER IS THE FIRST DISTINCT ROCK FORMATION ON THAT CREST, AND ITS NORTH-EAST FACE LOOKS BACK TOWARD THE PASS. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: THE MOUNTAIN LIES FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE, ABOVE A LAKE BASIN. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB ITSELF: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling LEFT into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the RIGHT, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The buttress toe is the LOW POINT of the prow, sitting immediately LEFT of the gully that separates North from South Early Winters Spire — so you find it by first locating that dividing gully and then stepping left out of it, rather than by heading straight up from the talus. The first pitch is rambling 5.6 with moss, dirt and some loose rock; a scruffy easy pitch is the correct start here, and if your first pitch is clean and steep you are too high on the buttress or on one of the harder east-side lines. The last large tree in the centre of Spire Gully is the checkpoint before this: if you are still climbing the gully and have passed no such tree, you have not reached the traverse point yet.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
approach_variants.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through Jun
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the buttress toe — it is still the low point of the prow just left of the North/South Early Winters dividing gully. What it changes is the traverse: on snow the rightward traverse from the last large tree in the gully is a straightforward but exposed snow crossing rather than a talus scramble, and the transition back onto rock at the base of the buttress will likely involve a moat. Fix the dividing gully visually from the highway before you start — from inside a snowy Spire Gully in flat light the individual features all read the same.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
approach_variants.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying BELOW the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
hazards: A moat around 7,000 ft that can close the route outright after mid-July
Icy gully beyond the notch in the morning — crampons are worth carrying for it
Steep dirt and very loose rock on the final five hundred feet
Rockfall from parties above on the hardpan and talus below the notch
No water at all above the Vista Lakes
Sloping slabs on the traverse from camp, avoidable by dropping to the scree around 6,000 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small NOTCH in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a MINOR ROCK RIDGE that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge IS the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its RIGHT, LOWER end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its WEST end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

NEGATIVE MARKER, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the FIRST and LEFT-MOST snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the UPPER RIGHT corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

THE MOAT IS THE GATE and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.

approach_variants.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
approach_variants.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
hazards: Windfall and vine maple on the bypass
No tread and no cairns
Same moat and loose-rock hazards above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The shortcut rejoins the standard line on the crest above and does not change where the climbing starts. Everything from the upper basin onward is as for the standard approach: the skyline notch to the west, the minor rock ridge running west-south-west across the base of the summit, the snow gap at its lower right end, and the moat around 7,000 ft as the real gate.

What you lose by taking it is the view of the peak that the PCT switchbacks give you on the way up, so identify the minor ridge and the notch from the basin rather than expecting to have already picked them out.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (snow-free)
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Great Scott Bowl, scramble to the notch just SOUTH of Pineapple Pass, then contour clockwise around the Tooth's south side. The last part of that contour is short class 3-4 and is not exposed; if it feels serious you are on the wrong ground.

You are at the start when you are standing under a broad, blocky face roughly 400 ft high with an obvious big vertical crack system splitting it. The first moves are easy ramps that angle LEFT to a large rectangular block, then back right into that crack system. About 100 ft up, the first belay is a slung rock horn with a balanced, flat-topped block sitting on it — that block is the confirmation you are on the standard line.

Two negative markers. If you are looking up a steep, narrow gully rather than an open face, you are in the gully between the Fang and the Tooth, one formation short — go back down and continue around. And if you scrambled straight up into a notch with rappel slings hanging above you, you are standing at Pineapple Pass on the descent route; downclimb and take the next notch south, then contour.

In early season a steeper gully runs up toward the base of the face. Do not use it unless it is filled with snow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
approach_variants.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
approach_variants.season: winter to early summer, snow
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The finish is the same: the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then a clockwise contour. Under snow the thing that decides where you can actually reach rock is the moat at the top of the bowl's snow. Probe it, and be ready to work around its edge on rock rather than force the direct step across.

With the base buried, the 'easy ramps left to a large rectangular block' start can be under snow. If you cannot find that block, you are probably below the true start — keep contouring around rather than climbing the first weakness above you, which is what puts parties into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes FS Road 28. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike SOUTH about 2 miles on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme in every account
Rockfall in the couloir between the twin summits, worst with parties above or after freeze-thaw
Glissade and uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout is not fully visible — one party described nearly going over a cliff band on nearby terrain
Faint use-trail-only route-finding above the trail through forest, meadow and talus
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS A CREEK YOU MUST NOT CROSS. Leave the trail BEFORE crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb EAST — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAMBED the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head NORTH to the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

THE TEST AT THE TOP OF THE COULOIR IS WHICH WAY TO TURN, AND IT IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE FOR THIS PEAK IN FOG: AT THE SADDLE, THE HIGHER PEAK IS ON YOUR RIGHT. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the RIGHT. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

SECOND TEST, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's NORTHWEST side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.

approach_variants.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
approach_variants.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb EAST into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Same as the Boulder Shelter variant: loose summit rock, couloir rockfall, glissade runout, faint route-finding
Home Lake sits below Constance Pass, so an exit north regains meaningful height before the long descent
Wilderness permit required and the site is popular with parties climbing four different peaks
approach_variants.baseFinding: FROM HOME LAKE THE TEST IS THE SAME STREAMBED, WORKED FROM THE OTHER END: leave the lake basin heading EAST into the cirque, STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAM that drains it. The stream is the handrail either way — approaching from Boulder Shelter you must not cross it, and approaching from the lake you must keep it below and to your right as you climb. THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME CLOSED CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and then the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS running north to the saddle at about 7,000 ft — the one gully with a summit on each side of it. AND THE SAME TURN AT THE TOP: AT THE SADDLE THE HIGHER, TRUE SUMMIT IS ON YOUR RIGHT (southeast). The 20 to 50 ft Class 4 / low fifth step on the block's northwest side is the last obstacle; if there is no step, you are on the northwest summit. HONEST LIMIT: this variant differs from the one above only in where you sleep and which direction you walk in. It is recorded separately because the route is titled for the Home Lake approach and a reader should not have to reconcile that with an approach description that starts from Boulder Shelter.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved most of the way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Nobody does this in a day; two nights out is the normal shape of the trip.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
hazards: No climbers' trail and no marked start; the base is identified by landform and by what is above you
Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured lower face
Afternoon storms on a summit that is the local high point
A walk-off descent whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
Remote enough that any injury becomes a multi-day evacuation
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no climbers' trail to the base. Cross the parkland and talus from camp toward the deep gully that divides Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower leaning against the lower right side of the wall. Thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

THE FIRST TEST IS THE TOWER, AND IT IS A NEGATIVE ONE. This route is on the MAIN wall, not on the tower and not on the buttress behind it. If a separate tower stands between you and the rock you are about to climb, walk further left along the base — you are under the Southeast Buttress. If you are looking up at an open thousand-foot face with nothing standing in front of it, you are in the right place.

Now place yourself across that face. This line takes the RIGHT-HAND portion of the open wall, between the central line and the line further right. There is no start ledge, no cairn and no fixed gear to find; the ground low down is heavily featured and the first ascent treated it as choose-your-own, so the start is a zone rather than a point. Pick the most featured rock in that right-hand third and go up.

CONFIRM IT ABOVE YOU BEFORE YOU COMMIT, because the low ground will accept almost any line. Look for a long ramp slashing rightward across the middle of the face, and above the ramp a steep, clean crack splitting a headwall. Those two features in that order are this route. If the ramp is not there and instead you find a big curving chimney above you, you have drifted into the centre of the wall and you are on the original central line — several number grades easier, and a different day.

Second negative marker, at the top: this route joins the buttress route for its final hand crack to the summit. Arriving at that shared pitch is correct. Arriving at it early, without having crossed a rightward ramp and pulled a thin headwall, means you traversed off.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a TRAIL, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way OUT, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip, on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
Beta headed South Face may describe the small tower rather than the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The way in changes; the base does not. From Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same walk toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, and the same question at the bottom: is there a tower standing between you and the rock? If yes you are under the buttress, not this face.

What this approach genuinely changes is your first sighting of the wall. Coming up the valley you arrive in the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side presents itself at once from across the water. Use that. Standing at the lake, pick out three things before you walk up: the tower at the lower right of the wall, the open thousand-foot face left of it, and the long ramp that slashes rightward across the middle of that face. This route is the right-hand third of the open face, working up to that ramp and to the steep crack in the headwall above it.

That identification is far easier from across the lake than from underneath, where the face foreshortens and the ramp disappears into the general featuring. Photograph it or draw it before you leave camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if from the lake you cannot see a ramp at all on the face you are looking at, you are looking at the wrong wall. The tower has its own south face with its own short routes on it, and beta written about that tower will also say South Face. The tower is small and stands clear of the mountain; the main face runs the full height of the peak behind it.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
approach_variants.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
hazards: About a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple on an officially abandoned path
A forested cut up the headwall to the right of the waterfall looks like the way and is not — taking it forces a Class 3/4 rock wall in the trees
The slab cut onto the glacier is easy snow early in the season and a gully with a stream running in it later, needing Class 2/3 slab work
The glacier is genuinely crevassed; roped travel with crevasse rescue capability is the expectation
Wet-loose runouts come off snow slabs perched on wet rock along the glacier margins
The moat crossing onto the summit rock varies through the season and can be the hardest move of the climb late in a dry year
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HEADWALL HAS A TEMPTING WRONG LINE ON IT, AND THE GLACIER HAS A TEMPTING WRONG LINE ABOVE IT. Coming up the basin the headwall looks formidable; the way up is at its far left, through a brushy gully where the headwall corners, and there is an appetising forested cut up the wall to the right of the waterfall that must not be taken — cutting right early forces you onto the low end of the rock wall in the trees. Above, steep forest veers right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft, where a piece of orange flagging has marked the way. Beyond that, a third and higher basin near 5,500 ft sits below the slabs of the receding glacier, and a natural cut on that basin's southwest side leads through the slabs onto the ice: easy snow early in the season, later a gully with a stream in it. Once on the glacier, the second trap: a snow and talus slope under the north side of the summit looks enticing and leads to the northeast ridge, which is far more exposed and saves nothing. Do not take it.

approach_variants.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
approach_variants.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Trackless climbing through open forest and slopes with no established line
The drop-in onto the glacier off the ridge has needed a rappel
Crevasses, and the season-dependent moat crossing onto the summit rock
The gentle-looking snowfield on the north side of the summit ridge ends in a dead vertical rock face
Many unbalanced rocks on the final crest, and cornices along it early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding: OPEN FOREST AND SLOPES, NOT BRUSH, IS THE SIGN YOU ARE ON THIS VARIANT. Leaving the crest trail farther south, the climb northwest gains roughly 3,500 ft through timber and open slope that stays walkable; if you are fighting slide alder and vine maple you have started up the Swamp Creek drainage instead and are on the older, much harder line. Veer left near the top of the drainage to reach the drop-in point onto the glacier — parties have needed a rappel to get off the ridge here, so carry the means to do it. Once on the ice, ignore the snow and talus slope running up under the north side of the summit: it looks enticing from the glacier and leads to the northeast ridge, which is much more exposed and saves no time. Leave the glacier by crossing the moat onto the rock instead, then take the three step-ups — up and left, up and left, up and left — to gain the west spur around 8,200 ft, east of the actual saddle.

approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

approach_variants.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek
approach_variants.notes: The other end of the same corridor, and the shorter way if Lizard is the objective rather than the traverse. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown — expect to step over and crawl under a great deal of it — with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt; scout for a log rather than committing to a wet crossing. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge, another established camp with tarn water, and from there the route goes cross-country across the South Cascade Glacier to top out at the col on Lizard's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
hazards: sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the South Cascade Glacier, worst late season once snow bridges have opened
multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
loose blocks near the summit crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. Coming up the South Cascade Glacier you top out in a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and the glacier you just left lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
approach_variants.notes:
