Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do NOT follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse BELOW the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
approach_variants.season: Best while Pea Soup Lake is still frozen and the moat is closed. The Pea Soup approach becomes problematic from mid-July onward once the ice melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LAKE YOU WALK ACROSS. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to FROZEN PEA SOUP LAKE. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

WHAT TO DO WHEN THE LAKE HAS MELTED OUT, WHICH IS THE COMMON CASE FROM MID-JULY: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge SEPARATING the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the FIRST MINOR NOTCH at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' LEFT via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

GETTING ONTO THE ICE, IN EITHER SEASON: early, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT. Late, bypass on climbers' LEFT by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

AND THE TOP TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT IS WHICH: the glacier leads to the GAP BETWEEN THE TWO HIGHEST SUMMITS. From the notch, the WEST summit — on your RIGHT — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A SCOPE NOTE THAT MATTERS TO PEAK-LIST PARTIES: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

approach_variants.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
approach_variants.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse WEST to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
approach_variants.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AIMING FOR THE OUTLET OF PEA SOUP LAKE, AND THE SHOULDER ABOVE THE FOSS RIVER IS THE WAYPOINT THAT GETS YOU THERE. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is WEST until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

FROM THE OUTLET THE FINDING IS THE SAME AS FROM PEGGY'S POND: get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' LEFT and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay RIGHT for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay LOW beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
hazards: Serac fall from the hanging ice cliff you traverse beneath — a party watched a large piece break away and shatter on the ledge below them
Rockfall and avalanche in the couloir
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the lower glacier
A cornice at the couloir exit, which becomes the crux when large
An unmaintained climbers' trail with blowdown and misleading cairns
Sporty log crossings of Mountaineer Creek, worse under early-season snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTH RIDGE ROCK RIB IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your RIGHT, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your LEFT, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the FOOT of the North Ridge, then cut hard LEFT and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

TOUCH TEST at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just BELOW the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.

approach_variants.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
approach_variants.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.
approach_variants.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
hazards: Avalanche on the approach slopes and in the couloir
Buried or unreachable log crossings
Deep postholing once off skis
Extra road mileage each way when the gate is down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification is the same and the North Ridge rib is still the thing to steer by — Sherpa left, Ice Cliff centre, the rib on your right, Stuart Glacier beyond it.

What changes in spring is that the frozen-debris touch test at the base may be buried or covered by fresh avalanche deposit, so it is less useful. Fall back on the geometry: you want to be under the ice cliff with the North Ridge rib immediately to your right, having cut left off the moraine at the foot of the rib rather than continuing up alongside it.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in the brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on the open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rough, narrow FR 4096 access spur
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your RIGHT for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
approach_variants.notes:
The start is an UNSIGNED climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk — deep, cold and fast in early season
Log jams that move year to year and cannot be relied on
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your RIGHT, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW AT CAMP. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS UPWARD FROM THE SADDLE TOWARD ROCK IS THE WRONG ONE.

IDENTIFY THE SADDLE FIRST: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

AT THE ICE, THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE BUTTRESS YOU GO UP. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS ITSELF, WHERE THE ROCK MEETS THE ICE ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE, IS THE START OF THE DIRECT AND NOT OF THIS ROUTE. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

WATCH THE JOIN BETWEEN SNOW AND ROCK. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A CROSS-CHECK ONCE COMMITTED: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It costs a legal border crossing, so passports and a plan for entering the country on foot are not optional, and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only with the paperwork in hand
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH VARIANT CHANGES ONLY HOW YOU ARRIVE AT THE 6,480 FT SADDLE. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by DROPPING off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

THE SAME TWO TESTS APPLY AT THE ICE. Go up the snow on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE MARKER: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
approach_variants.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
hazards: Several similar-looking gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
The steep rock-and-alder section above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the approach
Krummholz and vegetation-covered rock on the crux band
Teetering blocks near the summit
Days long enough that parties routinely finish the descent in the dark, with a boat pickup to make
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right GULLY out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

THE PHYSICAL TESTS ON THE CLIMB ITSELF ARE ROCK QUALITY AND TERRAIN GRADE, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with KRUMMHOLZ AND BLUFFS where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ENORMOUS AND UNMISTAKABLE. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

MARK YOUR EXACT ASCENT GULLY BEFORE YOU LEAVE IT, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
hazards: A long unpaved mountain road with 17 percent grades, no passing room and an unguarded drop
The road opens late and closes with the first autumn storms
Very long approach on foot with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary lies about a mile north of the summit and crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak is immediately to the north-east, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE ROCK. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and BEAR RIGHT at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear LEFT into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the EAST side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, so Trinity is currently not reachable by vehicle.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, so Trinity is currently unreachable by vehicle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NOTCH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S RIDGE, AND SAYING IT THAT WAY IS WHAT MAKES IT FINDABLE: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the NOTCH IN FORTRESS MOUNTAIN'S EAST RIDGE. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain NEXT DOOR, not toward the peak you are climbing.

WHAT THE LAST STRETCH FEELS LIKE, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

FROM THE COL THE ROUTE HAS NO SINGLE LINE AND THAT IS THE CORRECT ANSWER, NOT A GAP IN THE BETA: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXPLICIT AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class DEAD END. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

THE CRUX IS SHORT AND IT IS AT THE TOP: the step gaining the SUMMIT RIDGE is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the WEST — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

GOING BACK DOWN, USE A DIFFERENT LINE THAN YOU CAME UP FOR ONE STRETCH ONLY: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
approach_variants.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col WEST of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT'S BASE IS A DIFFERENT COL FROM THE MAIN ROUTE'S, AND CONFUSING THE TWO PUTS YOU ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The standard line goes to the FORTRESS-CHIWAWA col, which is SOUTH-WEST of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col WEST of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the RIGHT of Point 5971.

THE TEST IS WHAT LIES ABOVE THE COL YOU REACH. From this one, the WEST RIDGE runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west FACE with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

THE APPROACH MARKER IS A NUMBERED POINT AND THAT IS ALL THERE IS: the gully is to the RIGHT of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.
approach_variants.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
hazards: Loose scree and talus if you do not gain the moraine crest early
Rockfall off the surrounding faces onto the glacier, worst during the morning warm-up
Moats and thin bridging at the glacier margins
~100 ft of 40-degree snow below the col
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
Glissading the descent is normal here and is also how people get hurt — axe in hand, clear runout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route's 'base' is the toe of the glacier, at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, and the way to know you are there is that the moraine crest you have been walking runs out against continuous snow that keeps rising ahead of you.

From the toe, take the LEFT (east) lobe of the glacier. That side passes directly beneath the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes — seeing that big northwest wall on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct lobe. You are climbing beside those routes, not on them.

The glacier is easy angle for most of its length and then steepens for the last stretch: about 100 ft of 40-degree snow immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col (Colchuck Col / Banshee Pass) at roughly 8,200 ft. If the angle has not kicked back, you are not at the col yet.

From the col the summit is northwest: 3rd-class sandy steps up to a summit plateau around 8,500 ft, then continue west and north over the plateau to the true summit at 8,705 ft. The plateau is the trap in cloud — it is broad and flat and the first high ground you reach on it is not the summit.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
approach_variants.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
hazards: Bare sun-cupped ice: crampons and axe required, self-arrest unreliable
Open crevasses and moats at the glacier margins
Increased rockfall from the surrounding faces with no snow cover
No glissade descent — the day is longer at both ends
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The same landmarks, read differently. The toe of the glacier is further up the basin than it was in June — glacial retreat and seasonal melt both push it back — so the moraine crest walk is longer before you meet ice.

Stay on the LEFT (east) lobe under the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes. Late in the season a thin crevasse zone has been reported opening on the descent side, and parties are advised to stay climber's left of it coming down.

The steepening to about 40 degrees immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col at roughly 8,200 ft is still the marker that you have arrived, and on bare ice it feels considerably more serious than the same slope in snow.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
approach_variants.hours: 5-7 to high camp, 3-5 more to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount roughly 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area at about 2,100 ft. The first ten miles are paved; the rest is gravel and washboard.

The path does not leave from the parking area. Walk back down the road about 90 feet and look for the log (historically a large single log, sometimes a clump of trees) spanning the Cascade River. The crossing shifts year to year and is slick when wet — a handline is worth carrying for a party that is not confident on a log. On the far bank walk perpendicular to the river roughly 100 feet to pick up the boot path.

The path climbs steeply and relentlessly through old-growth timber with no water, gaining about 1,500 ft before it breaks out into the boulder field. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulders, staying climber's right so you do not cross Eldorado Creek unnecessarily. The boulder field is universally described as the worst part of the trip, and worse on the way down with a heavy pack.

Above the boulders the ground eases into Eldorado Creek Basin (roughly 5,400-5,600 ft, about 3 miles and 3,300 ft from the car), a common first camp. To continue, climb onto the rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft and drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (6,100-6,400 ft, running water). From Roush, broken talus and slabs lead onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier; rope up here. Moderate glacier slopes lead to high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle around 7,500-7,800 ft.

Overnight stays need a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. Eldorado is a high-use cross-country zone; there is an advance lottery and reservations on Recreation.gov, but permits for the areas off Cascade River Road (Eldorado, Boston Basin, Cascade Pass) must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the talus is bare
hazards: Cascade River log crossing — slick when wet, position shifts year to year
Boulder field is the crux of the walk, worse descending under a heavy pack
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, worsening as the day warms
Featureless flat glacier — whiteout navigation to The Gap
Exposed summit knife-edge; crevasses on the ridge crest itself
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start on this route — the climbing is the summit snow arete, and finding it means finding one gap on an otherwise featureless glacier.

From high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration saddle the Inspiration Glacier runs away nearly flat to the west. Cross it aiming for the obvious low gap in Eldorado's lower East Ridge, universally called 'The Gap'. Once you have stepped through the gap you are on the East Ridge; before that you are still on flat glacier.

The confirmation underfoot is that the ground stops being flat and becomes a defined crest, with glacier falling away on both sides rather than one. From the gap, go a short way further up onto the snow until a distinct ramp leads leftward/rightward onto the ridge crest proper — parties consistently report a gentle ramp reaching the base of the knife edge from its far right side. That ramp, and the point where the crest narrows so that both sides drop, is the base of the climbing.

The common error is stopping short: the flat Inspiration is genuinely disorienting in cloud, parties describe an hour of whiteout walking to reach the gap, and parties drift too low into crevassed glacier instead of holding the line to the low point on the skyline. Take and hold a bearing from camp. Later in the season the crest melts out and parties move onto the steeper snow slope to the right of the bare ridge, where crevasses open — early season the same crest can be broad enough to skin.

Stay roped on the ridge. It is not a rock ridge you have escaped the glacier onto; the line travels back onto glacier and crevasses exist on the crest itself.

approach_variants.name: Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
approach_variants.notes:
In late spring the upper approach is continuous snow and the boulder field problem largely disappears, which is why many parties prefer this window. It does not make the whole approach snow: a late-May park report described the route as snow-free until just before Eldorado Basin was gained around 5,000 ft, with the boulder fields completely melted out — so expect a dry, steep forest climb first and snow only above.

Ski parties commonly carry ski boots and walk the forest section in approach or running shoes, switching over at snow line.

The trade is avalanche exposure. Large avalanches sweep parts of this route in winter and spring, and Cascade River Road itself can be buried by avalanche debris miles below the trailhead in a heavy year, adding road miles before you even start.
approach_variants.season: late May-June
hazards: Avalanche paths across the approach and the road in spring
Snow-bridged creek channels in the lower basins — parties have punched through
Road may be closed or buried well below the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same gap in the lower East Ridge, but early season it is broader and more forgiving: the ridge is wide, sometimes wide enough to skin, and the knife edge that defines the route later in the summer may not have formed yet. Do not treat a wide, easy crest as evidence you are in the wrong place — the landmark is still The Gap, the low point on the ridge skyline reached by crossing the flat Inspiration.

approach_variants.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
approach_variants.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 5,400-6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
hazards: Sudden fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on an open above-treeline ridge with miles of exposure
Loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the crest
Lingering steep snowfields in north-facing gullies into July, warranting an ice axe
No reliable water once past the Baldy saddle spring
Long unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
The Gray Wolf River bridge on the alternative approach is out — a required and hazardous ford at high water
Bear canister required within Olympic National Park
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMB BEGINS WHERE THE TREAD ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SADDLE BETWEEN TYLER PEAK AND BALDY. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS ON THIS ROUTE IS AT THE FAR END, AND IT IS A FALSE SUMMIT WITH A NAME AND A NUMBER: POINT 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies FURTHER NORTH along the crest and is HIGHER. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and THAT BUMP IS NOT THE TOP. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

SECOND TEST, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to TRAVERSE WEST at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its NORTHWEST aspect, and to stay in the basin below and RIGHT of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

THIRD TEST, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally SKIRTED ON ITS SOUTH SIDE rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.

HONEST LIMIT: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
approach_variants.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the EXIT after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep, loose, lightly travelled ground with no established line and improvised anchors if roped
Roughly 3,000 ft of descent or ascent on packed dirt and shattered shale
Brushy notches and timber navigation looking for blazes and cairns
Committing: once on the east face there is no easy return to the crest
Every ridge-crest hazard above, in a longer day
approach_variants.baseFinding: USED AS AN APPROACH, THE ARRIVAL TEST IS GAINING THE CREST — and this side has no marker sequence for doing it. Parties describe finding blazes and cairns through timber rather than following a line. Treat it as navigation, not route-following. THE SUMMIT TESTS ONCE ON THE CREST ARE THE SAME AND THEY ARE THE VALUABLE PART: POINT 7076 IS A FALSE SUMMIT. Coming from the Royal Basin side you meet the true 7,218 ft summit from the north-east rather than from the south, so the trap runs the other way — the bump you must not stop on lies SOUTH of the true summit on this approach. Fix which side of you 7076 should be before you commit to the crest in cloud. HONEST LIMIT AND A RECOMMENDATION: this variant is known as a descent far more than as an ascent, and there is no fixed, repeatable rappel count for the cliffy step — expect at most one or two short rappels well under 60 m if you choose to rope, and expect most parties to downclimb or scree-ski instead. Confirm current conditions before relying on it either way.

approach_variants.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
approach_variants.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
hazards: a boundary crossing that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services
no water south of the creeks below the ridge junction
an exposed ridge camp
a 545 ft descent from camp that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
loose rock on the buttress
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CAMP THE ROUTE STARTS BY LOSING HEIGHT - ABOUT 545 FT DOWN TO THE 5,800 FT SADDLE AT THE HEAD OF THE NORTH CIRQUE. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS FROM THE CAMP IS THE WRONG WAY. The saddle is the low point at the head of a bowl, with the cirque falling away in front of you and the buttress rising on its far side.

RECOGNISE THE CIRQUE BY ITS SHAPE: it is an enclosed bowl beneath the north side of the peak, not an open flank. If the ground ahead of you drops away into a valley rather than into a bowl with walls around it, you have gone off the ridge too early or too late.

THE BUTTRESS IS ON THE NORTH-EAST SIDE, so from the saddle it should stand between you and the sun in the middle of the day rather than in it. A wall you approach in full afternoon sun is on the wrong aspect.

CHECK THE PEAK: this is the NORTH summit, the higher and broader of the two. The other main summit should lie to the south, connected by a rotten ridge that is not a usable link between them.

WATER IS THE OTHER FIXED POINT. The last of it is the creeks in the forest below the ridge junction, well before camp. If you have passed those without filling, the correct move is to go back for water rather than to press on to a dry camp above a dry cirque.

approach_variants.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
hazards: an overgrown boundary swath that is steep, brushy and slow
a swamp low on the line
three thousand feet of unrelenting bushwhacking with no tread
no water on the upper half
reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SWATH IS THE HANDRAIL - IT IS A CLEARED LINE THROUGH FOREST THAT RUNS EAST, AND IF YOU ARE NOT ON IT YOU ARE NOT ON THE APPROACH. It is overgrown, so it looks like brush rather than like a corridor from inside it; the tell is that it is straight, and it does not wander with the terrain the way a game trail does.

A SWAMP IS PASSED LOW DOWN. Reaching it confirms the line; never reaching it means you have drifted off the swath into ordinary forest.

THE JOIN IS A COL NEAR 6,300 FT, roughly three thousand feet above the start, where the swath's climbing ends against the ridge. From there the route is the same as the long approach: work along to the saddle at the head of the north cirque near 5,800 ft, WHICH MEANS LOSING HEIGHT AGAIN, and the buttress stands on the far side of the bowl.

IF YOU ARRIVE ON A RIDGE AND THE GROUND BEYOND IS AN OPEN VALLEY RATHER THAN AN ENCLOSED BOWL, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG COL. The cirque is walled; the valley is not.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the very start, which has washed out
long waterless switchbacks on both trail sections
crevasses and moats on the Jerry Glacier, worse as a bare-ice slip hazard late in the season
fire-damaged forest and unstable ground near Jerry Lakes
loose rock on the face where holds pull off freely - keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked
route-finding for the ramp and hidden chimney, which are hard to relocate on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FACE IS FOUND BY A SLUNG BOULDER AND A HIDDEN BREAK, NOT BY A BEARING. From the Jerry Lakes basin, traverse the heather shelf and go through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,000 to 7,200 ft. THIS SHOULDER IS THE DECISION POINT FOR THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN. For the South Face you now turn WEST and make a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, often moving in the shallow moat where old snow has pulled away from the rock.

THE POSITIVE MARKER IS A BOULDER WITH SLING MATERIAL ON IT, standing above the snow patches under the lower cliff band. The break in that band is a left-slanting ramp leading to a short class 4 step and then a hidden class 3 chimney, and IT STAYS INVISIBLE UNTIL YOU ARE ALMOST UNDERNEATH IT. Looking up from a distance and seeing no way through the band is the normal experience and is not evidence you are in the wrong place; looking up and seeing an obvious open gully is evidence that you are, because the break here is not obvious.

IF YOU ARE CLIMBING THE CREST OF THE RIDGE ITSELF RATHER THAN TRAVERSING BENEATH A FACE, YOU HAVE STAYED ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE AND ARE ON THE OTHER ROUTE. The South Face leaves the ridge at the shoulder and does not return to it until well above the cliff band, near 8,600 ft, where a band of scree beside a snow patch delivers you back onto the crest.

A CROSS-CHECK ABOVE THE BAND: 400 to 500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges linked by harder steps, then easier ground. Sustained hard climbing straight off the chimney means you have taken the wrong line through the band.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent. Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of Crater Creek Basin if you camp low
no water above the lakes or the meadows
exposed camps with weather coming over the crest
loose ground on the traverse under the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE LEVEL SHOULDER ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE NEAR 7,000 TO 7,200 FT. From the lakes you reach it by crossing the notch south of the lakes and climbing back out of Crater Creek Basin; from the meadows camp you climb straight to it.

THE SHOULDER IS RECOGNISED BY BEING LEVEL. The ridge relents here into a flat step before it rears up again, and the ground to the west opens into the scree traverse under the face. If you are still climbing steadily with no let-up, you are below it.

FROM THE SHOULDER THE SOUTH FACE GOES WEST AND DOWN-SLOPE OF THE CREST, ON SCREE AND DIRT, TOWARD SNOW PATCHES AND A SLUNG BOULDER UNDER A CONTINUOUS CLIFF BAND. If you find yourself scrambling directly up the crest above the shoulder you are on the Southeast Ridge line instead - a legitimate route, but not this one, and it has no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on it.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, at about 5,200 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about a mile and a half. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (dry)
hazards: loose rock and party-induced rockfall in the notch gully — helmets on before entering, and avoid stacking up under other parties
steep 3rd-class steps on the climbers' path when wet
trailhead lot fills early on summer weekends; roadside parking on SR-20 is limited
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start climbing from the notch itself. The first pitch begins from a tree standing roughly 30 feet BELOW the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, on the Liberty Bell (north) side. From that tree a small ledge runs left; walk it and it delivers you to the foot of a blocky chimney, and that chimney is pitch one. If you are stood on the low point of the notch looking for a crack going straight up, you are too high and too far right — drop back down to the tree. Concord Tower's North Face starts from the top of the same notch, on the opposite (south) wall, so two parties can be at the same notch climbing in opposite directions; check which wall you are facing before you rack up.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
hazards: firm or refrozen snow in the gully — a slip runs a long way over rock
moat at the transition from snow to rock at the base of the first pitch
wet-loose and cornice debris in the gully during spring melt
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access to the trailhead until the highway reopens
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow changes what the last hundred metres looks like. With the gully filled, the notch reads as a clean snow finish rather than a scree saddle, and the tree that marks the Beckey start — about 30 feet below the crest on the Liberty Bell side, with a small ledge running left to the blocky chimney — can be partly buried or standing above a moat. If you top out onto the notch crest and find no tree, you have gone above the start; downclimb the last stretch on the Liberty Bell side and look for it. Expect a moat where snow pulls away from the rock at the base of the chimney.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River Trail from Salmon La Sac
approach_variants.notes: The southern approach, and a long one — most parties treat it as a two- or three-day trip rather than a push. From the Salmon La Sac road end, take the Waptus River trail east into the wilderness. The first mile rolls over low forested hills before the trail settles into a long gentle grade beside the river, crossing many small feeder creeks — water is reliable the whole way — and skirting boggy meadow and old burn. Around the seven-to-eight mile mark stay on the Waptus River trail rather than forking north toward Spade Lake. The river crossing below Waptus Lake is a genuine FORD: the old hiker bridge washed out and was never replaced, so expect knee-deep water in normal summer flow. Past the outlet the trail runs the lake's southeast shore, a stretch that holds steep snow into early summer. Continue toward Lake Ivanhoe and the Chief Creek drainage; most parties camp near the Chief Creek ford.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The lakeshore stretch holds steep snowfields into early summer and the river ford is far more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford near the lake — cold, swift, and far more serious in snowmelt
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Loose scree and route-finding, rather than any single obstacle, as the main hazard on the upper slopes
Exposed low-fifth-class notch below the summit ridge that some parties rope
Loose rock throughout — no fixed or bolted anchors are reported anywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the Chief Creek crossing, faint switchbacks climb open slopes toward the peak's west ridge. The base of the climbing proper is where the TREES STOP: below the treeline you are on a trackable, if faint, boot line, and above it there is no tread at all, only continuous heather benches and talus with loose scree — that transition is the start, and there is no cairn, anchor or marker at it. The confirming feature comes much higher and is the one technical spot on the route: the final few hundred feet narrow onto an exposed summit ridge with a NARROW ROCK NOTCH just below the top, and if your line never reaches a notch you have drifted off it. Negative markers: if you are on maintained tread, you have not left the Waptus River trail yet; if you find yourself on the far side of the mountain looking down a valley toward a steel bridge on a river trail, you have crossed the divide into the Middle Fork drainage and are above the routes approached from the north.

approach_variants.name: Direct creek line below Lake Ivanhoe
approach_variants.notes: A commonly cited variation that shortens the upper approach. Rather than continuing all the way to the Chief Creek camp, leave the main trail a short distance south of Lake Ivanhoe and follow the creek that drains from there into the Waptus River, gaining the peak's west side more directly. Everything below that point is identical to the standard approach, including the river ford.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: No path at all above the trail; the creek is the only handrail
Loose scree and brush on the lower slopes
Same unbridged Waptus ford and snow-holding lakeshore as the standard approach
Exposed notch below the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Leave the trail where the creek draining toward the Waptus meets it, a short distance south of Lake Ivanhoe, and use the creek as your handrail — the creek line IS the route-finding, because there is no path. The base of the climbing is again the point where the timber thins out and the ground becomes unbroken heather bench and talus running up toward the west ridge crest. The check that you are on the right drainage is that it leads you up onto the WEST side of the peak, with the summit ridge above and to your right as you climb. Negative marker: if the creek is taking you away from the peak rather than under it, or you find yourself dropping toward a lake, you are on the wrong drainage — this line gains ground continuously from the moment you leave the trail.

approach_variants.name: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 to Upper Eagle Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the forest-road spur, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit and start up Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The tread crosses Crater Creek on a bridge early on — stay straight where the Crater Creek Trail splits — and climbs steadily, with an established camp roughly halfway. Past an overlook of the lower lake the trail reaches a junction: the left branch goes to the lower lake and the pass beyond, the right-hand spur climbs a half mile to Upper Eagle Lake. Take the spur. The upper lake sits in a cirque with established campsites and is the last reliable water and the staging point before the off-trail push, which starts from its northwest shore.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through October, once road and trail are snow-free. Snow lingers in the notch through the lower cliff band into summer and makes the route-finding harder.
hazards: Route-finding through the cliff bands is genuinely tricky, especially with snow still lying in the notch
Steep, loose scree and rock between the bands, with a loose path worn straight up it
Pushing too far climber's right onto the better rock cliffs you out at the end of the ridge
An eight-foot chimney below the summit block with poor handholds in small pebbles and sand — a slip there would be serious
The summit rises over 1,300 ft above the upper lake in about a third of a mile
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: GO UP THROUGH THE LARCHES AND VEER RIGHT TO THE NOTCH, THEN CUT LEFT UNDER THE NEXT BAND. From Upper Eagle Lake a path runs round the lake; above it the landmark is vegetation rather than rock. Climb up through the larch stand and veer right to a notch, then take easy slabby rock to get above the lower cliff band. Once above it, head LEFT, staying beneath the next band, and only when past that is it a straight push up steep scree and rock to just below the summit block. That alternation — right through the larches, then left under the upper band — is the shape of the route, and the error parties actually make is the opposite: the better, more stable rock lies further climber's right and tempts parties onto it, where they get cliffed out at the end of the ridge and have to downclimb. At the block itself, look for a notch with a chimney step of about eight feet and a sandy gully above it. The step is climbed upward and its top holds are poor, in small pebbles and sand; there is an easier scramble round to the LEFT at its base that rejoins the sandy gully just above the chimney, and taking it is the difference between a committing move and a walk.

approach_variants.name: Horsehead Pass and the west slopes
approach_variants.notes: The easier alternative stays on the main trail past the Upper Eagle Lake spur, continues to the lower lake and climbs to Horsehead Pass, then gains the peak's west slopes from the far side of the crest. It trades the exposed scrambling for distance and a long, loose walk-up, and is the sensible choice for a party that does not want the cliff-band route-finding or that finds snow still lying in the notch above the upper lake.
approach_variants.season: July through October. The west side melts out and stays passable later in the autumn than the shaded notch on the east side.
hazards: Long and described as annoyingly loose underfoot for its whole length
No water once you leave the lake basin
Exposed crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: THIS LINE IS IDENTIFIED BY WHAT IT DOES NOT HAVE: NO CLIFF BANDS AND NO SCRAMBLING. Carry on past the spur to the upper lake, stay on the main trail to the lower lake, and climb to Horsehead Pass on the crest. From the pass the peak's west slopes rise as continuous open scree and broken rock with a walkable line the whole way and nothing that needs hands. That is the confirmation you are on the right side of the mountain. If you find yourself traversing beneath a band of slabby rock, threading a notch, or looking at a short exposed step down into a sandy gully, you have ended up on the direct line from the upper lake instead and should reconsider whether the party is equipped for it. The west slopes are looser and longer than they look from the pass, so the trade is real: this variant removes the scrambling and adds a great deal of tedious ground.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3.5 for the Lake Constance trail alone
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5-6 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations available roughly mid-June to mid-October; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: START UP THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS COME INTO VIEW, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

The chute climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.

approach_variants.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
approach_variants.notes:
The 5-6 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the unsigned start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable roughly mid-June to mid-October, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path
approach_variants.baseFinding: Unchanged from the walk-in: around the lake, north into Avalanche Canyon, and up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears appear above you, with the Thumb on the canyon's left marking the chute's south side. The Cat Ears becoming visible is the trigger to start climbing, not a landmark to walk toward.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
hazards: loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, worst near the summit saddle and the final gully
a steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
a long, mostly off-trail final leg with no marked line
afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NOTCH IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE BLOCK FROM WHERE YOU ARRIVE, AND YOU HAVE TO TRAVERSE TO IT. Whichever approach you used, the climbing starts the same way. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the EAST side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, SHALLOW gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height.
