The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
approach_variants.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: cliff bands around 5,200 ft where the crest is blocked and the bypass is on climber's right — the main route-finding failure on this side
a steep snow finger on this flank into early summer, with wet-slide and sluff potential
brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
an exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NOTCH IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE BLOCK FROM WHERE YOU ARRIVE, AND YOU HAVE TO TRAVERSE TO IT. Whichever approach you used, the climbing starts the same way. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the EAST side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, SHALLOW gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height. The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

approach_variants.name: Paradise to Camp Muir, then Cathedral Gap and Ingraham Flats
approach_variants.notes:
Paradise (5,420 ft) is the trailhead. Maintained tread on the Skyline Trail runs past Panorama Point (~6,800 ft) and Pebble Creek (~7,200 ft) — Pebble Creek is the last running water on the route — and ends near McClure Rock (~7,385 ft). Everything above that is the Muir Snowfield, which the Park Service does not mark or maintain; the trench you follow is boot-packed and wanded by the guide services and is erased by wind or new snow within hours.

The snowfield is the part of this route that kills people who are not climbing. It is a narrow tongue with heavily crevassed glaciers on both flanks — Nisqually to the west, Cowlitz to the north and east, Paradise to the south and east — and the cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock is corniced and snow-covered in winter. A modest navigation error puts you on a glacier or over an edge. The Park Service publishes bearings for this ground for that reason: north of Pebble Creek the line to Moon Rocks runs 355 degrees true. Carry map and compass and know the bearings before the visibility goes.

Camp Muir (10,080 ft) is the high camp: stone huts, a public shelter, a ranger station and toilets on a saddle between the snowfield and the Cowlitz Glacier. Nightly capacity is capped and the camp fills, especially Friday and Saturday. Ingraham Flats and the snowfield itself are the sanctioned overflow, each with a much smaller cap.

Permits: everyone on a glacier or above roughly 10,000 ft needs a per-person climbing permit for the calendar year, obtained online or at a ranger station. Overnights during the high-use season need a wilderness permit for the specific camp, with roughly half the capacity reservable in advance and the balance held for walk-ups; a reservation still has to be picked up in person. Party size is two or more unless you hold a rare solo authorisation.

From Camp Muir the day begins roped. Cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier eastward toward the Cathedral Rocks, pass through Cathedral Gap — the breach in that rock ridge — and drop into Ingraham Flats (~11,200 ft), a bench under the Ingraham icefall used both as a rest stop and as an alternative high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late May through September, once guide services have the boot track in
hazards: Whiteout navigation on the Muir Snowfield — unmarked, unmaintained, glaciers and cliffs on both flanks, boot track erased by wind
Corniced cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock, hidden under snow in winter
Crevasses on the Cowlitz crossing between Camp Muir and Cathedral Gap
Rockfall in Cathedral Gap and off the Cleaver, worst once the sun is on it
Serac fall from the Ingraham icefall above Ingraham Flats
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts where you step off snow onto the rock of the Cleaver, and there are three checks that you are in the right place.

First, direction out of Camp Muir. You should be crossing the Cowlitz eastward and gaining a notch in a rock ridge — Cathedral Gap. If instead you are climbing a rock ridgeline immediately northwest of camp, out of the tents, you are on the Cowlitz Cleaver and you are on the Gibraltar Ledges approach, a different route.

Second, the Flats. Ingraham Flats is genuinely flat — a bench with dug tent platforms and the Ingraham icefall hanging above and to the west. If you are still gaining steadily and have not walked across level ground, you have not reached it.

Third, the Cleaver itself. From the Flats you traverse to the Cleaver's lower southern side. You do not climb the nose. The nose is the low rock toe pointing down at the Flats, and the boot track passes it and gains rock roughly 300 ft above it, on the Ingraham side. If you are pulling onto rock at the very lowest point of the rib you are off the track. Once on it, you are on a rock rib with glacier on both sides and you follow it to its top at about 12,300 ft.

Negative marker: if the whole way from the Flats stays on snow with the icefall directly overhead and you never touch rock, you are on the Ingraham Direct, not the Cleaver.

approach_variants.name: High camp at Ingraham Flats instead of Camp Muir
approach_variants.notes:
Ingraham Flats (~11,200 ft) is a permitted camp with a much smaller nightly cap than Camp Muir, and it is the sanctioned overflow when Muir is booked out. The approach is identical as far as Camp Muir; you then rope up and continue over the Cowlitz and through Cathedral Gap with camp gear, which turns the carry into a longer day but removes about 1,100 ft and the Cathedral Gap crossing from summit morning.

The trade is exposure. The Flats sit under the Ingraham icefall, and the camp is chosen and re-sited by the rangers with that in mind. There is no water, no shelter and no toilet building; the Camp Muir facilities are 1,100 ft below you.
approach_variants.season: Same window; used when Camp Muir is full or to shorten summit day
hazards: Serac fall from the Ingraham icefall onto the camp and the ground immediately above it
No water source and no shelter at the Flats
Camp capacity is small and separately permitted from Camp Muir
approach_variants.baseFinding: Camping here puts you within a few hundred metres of the Cleaver's base, so the recognition problem changes shape: you are looking for the traverse line off the bench rather than for the bench itself. From the tents, the Cleaver is the rock rib bounding the Flats on the north and west. Walk toward its lower southern flank and expect to gain rock a few hundred feet above its lowest toe, not at the toe. Icefall debris on the snow between camp and the rib is a sign you are crossing under the serac line rather than skirting it — that ground is to be crossed quickly and not lingered on.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek roadbed, then the ridgecrest opposite the ski area
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest DIRECTLY OPPOSITE THE SKI AREA, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day. It was climbed in 2007 by a party who took sixteen hours on the 1,300 ft arête alone, having started from the White Salmon Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This is the more direct of the two options and it is a bushwhack, so it wants the ground clear rather than snow-covered
hazards: Bushwhacking with no tread, where a wrong drainage costs a day
Runout climbing on loose rock high on the arête
Moderate alpine ice and extensive glacier travel on the same outing as the rock
A very long day: the first-ascent party took sixteen hours on the arête itself
A descent that exits down the upper and lower White Salmon Glacier rather than reversing the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SKI AREA IS THE ONE THING YOU CAN SEE FROM ANYWHERE, AND IT IS THE AIMING MARK. The crest you want is the one directly opposite the ski area across White Salmon Creek. Cross the creek, climb, and stop when you are on a crest with the ski area behind you and level with you. In flat light that back-bearing is more reliable than anything ahead of you, because the ski area's cut runs and lift lines are the only man-made shape in the drainage.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROUTE ITSELF: the crest is a ramp, not the climb. Follow it until it runs into the mountain's north side, and the arête proper is the pillar the crest delivers you to. It is roughly 1,300 ft of climbing above that point.

DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTES EITHER SIDE OF IT: this is a ROCK PILLAR, not a glacier and not a snow face. If the ground in front of you at the base is a glacier you are looking at the White Salmon; if it is a broad snow-and-ice face you are looking at the North Face. The northwest arête is the pillar between them, and the first ground you touch on it is rock.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the valley past the point where the opposite crest is climbable puts you on the other variant — up the valley to the lower White Salmon Glacier. That is a legitimate approach, but it is a different one, and mixing the two mid-way leaves you sidehilling.

approach_variants.name: Up the White Salmon valley to the lower glacier, then onto the crest
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same parking: continue up the road as far as it goes, then travel off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier, and gain the crest of the arête from there.

It trades the creek crossing and the direct climb to the crest for more valley travel and a glacier approach. Parties choosing between the two are choosing between bushwhack-then-ridge and valley-then-glacier; both are documented and neither is a shortcut.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the lower White Salmon
Off-trail valley travel with no tread and brush low down
Loose rock and runout climbing on the arête above
Complex route-finding described by the first-ascent party as one of the route's defining features
No quick retreat: the descent is a separate glacier descent, not a reverse of the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER IS THE HANDRAIL, AND YOU LEAVE IT WHEN THE ROCK STARTS. Stay in the valley until the slopes open enough to walk onto the lower White Salmon Glacier, then work up the glacier with the arête's rock on your side and step onto it where the two meet.

THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT is the same one the direct variant uses, from the other direction: at the base of this route you are on ROCK, with the White Salmon Glacier on one side of the pillar and the North Face ground on the other. If you can still see glacier on both sides of you, you have not stepped onto the arête yet.

WHAT DROPPING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: if the valley narrows and you are still in trees and brush with no open slope, you have not gone far enough up-valley to reach the glacier access, and pushing sideways onto the mountain from there puts you on steep vegetated ground below the pillar rather than at its foot.

AND THE ORIENTATION CHECK: the descent for this route comes down the upper and then the lower White Salmon Glacier and deposits you back in this drainage. If your intended base is somewhere you could not plausibly walk back to down a glacier on this side, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with a register at the obelisk
a road that washes out and lengthens the walk without warning
wet slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls, with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
crevasses on the south-west glacier and one marginal snow bridge on the standard line
a short steep loose gully at the head of the glacier
thirty-five to forty degree snow near the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CRITICAL INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU LEAVE THE DRAINAGE BEFORE THE PASS, NOT AT IT. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but WELL BEFORE reaching that saddle, cut RIGHT around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXACT AND EASY TO USE: IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE SADDLE AND ARE LOOKING DOWN INTO THE CIRQUE ON THE FAR SIDE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

THE BUTTRESS TOE IS THE FEATURE - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

THE BASE IS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. THE LINE UP THE ICE IS ITS CLIMBER'S-RIGHT MARGIN, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

CONFIRM AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the cabin
a long carry to a high camp
crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide
a camp position that makes descriptions written from the other approach misleading
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE OLD CABIN AT ABOUT 2,900 FT IS THE PROOF YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE CREEK. The trail climbs the NORTH side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

ABOVE THE CABIN THE MARKERS ARE OCCASIONAL BLAZES ON TREES rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

THE CAMP IS THE LAKE BASIN AT ABOUT 6,763 FT, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

BE CLEAR WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON WHEN YOU ARRIVE. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE INSTEAD WANTS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, WHICH IS REACHED BY TRAVERSING INTO OPEN HEATHER AND MORAINE BASINS ROUND THE TOE OF A ROCK BUTTRESS, NOT BY GAINING A COL. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
approach_variants.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (east) about a mile to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
hazards: Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade
Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind
The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above
Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk
The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Look at the mountain from Longs Pass and settle the line there. It is the only point on the approach where the entire south face is laid out in front of you, and once you have dropped to the valley floor at 4,800 ft the couloir's mouth is one of several timbered gully mouths that all look alike from below and from inside the trees.

What you are aiming for: the couloir bottoms out in the meadow at roughly 4,800 ft, upvalley (east) of where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, and a beaten climbers' path leaves the meadow directly into it. It is a wide, sandy, scree-floored trough rather than a narrow cleft, and it runs unbroken for about 4,000 ft.

The confirmation that you are in the right gully comes about two thirds of the way up: a permanent snowfield around 8,800 ft, just south of the false summit. The established talus path passes it on the CLIMBER'S LEFT. Parties who take the right-hand side of that snowfield end up on much harder ground and have found old rappel-station remnants there — that is the tell that you have gone wrong, not a sign you are on route.

The couloir does not top out on the summit. It delivers you to the false summit at about 9,200 ft; the true summit at 9,415 ft is a class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge from there, and this is the second place parties in cloud go wrong — stopping at the false summit, or dropping off it in the wrong direction on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
approach_variants.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
hazards: FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out
Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself
South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional
Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass
Uncontrolled glissade on descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow cover the couloir reads far more clearly from the valley than it does in summer — it is the continuous white ribbon running the full height of the south face, and the timbered gully mouths that confuse people in August are buried. Still take the look from Longs Pass, because the valley-floor approach is in trees.

The 8,800 ft snowfield that is a landmark in summer is not a distinct feature when everything is snow, so the useful marker on the way up is the false summit at about 9,200 ft where the couloir ends. Do not treat topping out as summiting; the true summit is a scramble further east along the ridge.

On the descent in these conditions the risk inverts: the couloir is a glissade or boot-ski for most of its length and parties overrun themselves. Keep the axe in hand.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 roughly 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, trend LEFT of the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, and work up into the gully that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route does not start from the high point of the col. From the crest, move slightly WEST and drop a couple of feet: the first pitch begins at an obvious slanting, right-leaning crack in the Lexington side of the notch, and the 5.7 crux is the very first thing you climb — awkward moves straight off the ground. Follow the leaning crack for about 15 to 20 feet and it eases into stemming up a chimney at around 5.6. If your first moves are easy you are probably on the Concord wall opposite, which is the South Face of Concord and starts by walking gravelly ledges rather than pulling on a crack. A hard start on a right-leaning crack, just below and west of the col, is the confirmation.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through late Jun
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow in the col the slanting crack that starts the route can be partly buried, and the couple of feet of drop west from the high point may instead be a step down into a moat. The feature to hold onto is that the start is on the LEXINGTON side, slightly west of and just below the crest, at a right-leaning crack, and the hardest climbing of the first pitch is immediately off the deck. If snow has filled the crack's base, expect to start higher up it than the summer start and to be dealing with wet rock for the first body length.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay CLIMBER'S LEFT (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east and south through the Core's tarns and slabs to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right into the cliffed waterfall terrain has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of Aasgard, worse in the afternoon heat
Misleading and multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Very long day; parties routinely finish the descent of Aasgard in the dark
Descent from Prusik is rappels, not a walk-off — do not arrive without the gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do NOT go over the first bump in front of you — go AROUND it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge BALANCED, DISH-SHAPED ROCK — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an OVERHANGING ROCK at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a WIDE CRACK, about 5.6, in a conspicuously WHITE section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
approach_variants.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice
Uncontrolled slide on the pass, ascending or descending
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go AROUND the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — early season, snow gully
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3 to camp, about 2.5 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as everything else in Boston Basin: the unsigned pullout on Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile, then the sharp right onto the steep climbers' trail. Four stream crossings, then treeline at about 5,300 ft. Low camp on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft, higher camp on the knoll at about 6,300-6,400 ft.

From camp, skirt climber's left of the Quien Sabe Glacier and gain it relatively high, then rope up and traverse east/climber's right along the top of the glacier several hundred feet until you are directly beneath the tower.

Early season the approach gully is snow, around 35 degrees, and is the pleasant version of this approach — crampons and an axe, straightforward booting. A bergschrund or seracs can bar the direct entry; class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate way in that rejoins the gully about a hundred feet up.

Do the identification work on the walk in, not at the base. The whole sequence — glacier, gully, terrace and notch — is visible from the lower Boston Basin trail and from camp. Look at it in good light while you still have perspective on it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while the approach gully still holds snow
hazards: Wrong-gully error — the defining hazard of this approach, with a fatal precedent
Bergschrund or seracs barring the direct gully entry
Rockfall in the gully, natural and from parties above
Poor natural anchors — a boulder anchor failure caused the 2005 fatalities
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe traverse
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the most consequential base-finding problem on this list, and it has killed people.

The correct line: from a position on the glacier directly below the tower — not past it — a single gully breaks through the steep rock band. Follow it up to a snow patch or sloping terrace at the base of the tower. From that terrace, a short second gully leads to a notch, and the notch is the start of the Southeast Ridge. Some parties also describe a snow gully west of the tower that gives access to that same wide bench below the objective.

The test to apply before committing: does this gully put me on a terrace directly under the fin? If you are climbing a gully that trends away from being underneath the tower, you are in the wrong one. Being on rock is not evidence of being on route — there are similar-looking gullies here.

On 10 July 2005 a six-person party crossed the glacier, walked past the standard access gully and climbed a similar-looking gully further along. The traverse back toward the correct line put them under rockfall, which struck a climber; during the retreat rappel a natural boulder anchor failed. Three died and a fourth was seriously injured. Every subsequent description of this approach leads with the same instruction: identify the correct gully.

Carry a beta photo or a GPS track. In cloud, when you cannot see the fin above you, this approach should not be committed to on guesswork.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — late season, dry gully
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical. What changes is the gully: by late summer the snow is gone and it is loose scree and rubble, manageable but tedious and much more prone to knocking rock onto whoever is below. Trekking poles replace crampons.

The other late-season change is the moat where the glacier meets rock at the gully's base, which opens up as the season goes on and can require a committing step or a short awkward move onto rock.

One recorded late-season day trip left town at 4am, was in Boston Basin by about 8:30am, traversed underneath the tower to find the approach gully, and reached the notch before 11am.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the gully has melted out
hazards: Wrong-gully error, harder to rule out once the snow has gone
Loose scree and climber-triggered rockfall in the gully
Open moat at the glacier-rock junction
Rockfall from parties rappelling the descent line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification rule does not change: the correct gully is the one directly beneath the tower that delivers you onto the sloping terrace at the fin's base, followed by a short gully to the notch that begins the Southeast Ridge.

Late season it is arguably harder to be sure, because the snow that made the gully obvious from a distance has gone and several dry rubble chutes look alike from the glacier. Rely on the view from lower down: the gully, terrace and notch are all visible from the approach trail and from camp, so fix the line in your head before you lose the perspective.

Descent parties commonly rappel part of the route and then off rock to the west of the approach gully, so a fixed station west of your gully is a supporting sign you are in the right corridor — but it is a weaker signal than the terrace itself.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CAMP IS FOUND BY REFUSING A SUMMIT. The climbers' path leads toward Pyramid Peak and the correct move is to drop slightly BEFORE it and traverse across scree and boulders to the moraine. IF YOU HAVE SCRAMBLED TO A SUMMIT, YOU HAVE CLIMBED THE WRONG PEAK AND GONE PAST THE TRAVERSE. The arrival marker is a meltwater tarn sitting against a terminal moraine with the ice above it.

FROM CAMP THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE PIECES OF GROUND AND THEY MUST COME IN ORDER. First, rope up before leaving camp and climb the Colonial Glacier south past a rock feature on its east flank, on snow up to about thirty degrees, working around the moraine lake to a broad col near 6,840 ft. A STREAM RUNS AT THAT COL - a saddle with no water on it is not the right one.

Second, from the col you DROP roughly 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. IF YOU ARE STILL GAINING HEIGHT AFTER THE COL, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE CROSSING. This is the stretch with no reference points, so track your line for the return; whiteout navigation here is the standing problem of the route.

Third, leave the glacier on the peak's NORTH-WEST side near a prominent rock feature around 7,700 ft and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. That puts you three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit. IF YOU ARE STILL ON ICE WITH THE SUMMIT PYRAMID RISING STRAIGHT ABOVE YOU AND NO GULLY BESIDE IT, YOU HAVE CROSSED TOO FAR AND ARE UNDER THE FACE RATHER THAN THE RIDGE.

The finish is a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and blocky scrambling. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.

approach_variants.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
approach_variants.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS IDENTIFIED BY THREE THINGS AT ONCE: it is broad, it has a stream on it, and the ground beyond it DROPS onto a second, much larger glacier. A saddle that is dry, or one with nothing but rock beyond it, is not this col.

FROM CAMP THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL - 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve - and then a roped crossing on which the cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field. Bridges are usually sound by midsummer and need active route-finding around open slots. MARK YOUR OUTBOUND LINE. Coming back to a col you cannot see, across ground with no features, is the part of this route that goes wrong.

LEAVE THE ICE ON THE PEAK'S NORTH-WEST SIDE around 7,700 ft, near the prominent rock feature there, and take the class 3 gully with its single exposed rib crossing onto the west ridge, three to four hundred feet below the summit. IF THERE IS NO GULLY WHERE YOU STEP OFF THE ICE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR ACROSS.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved almost all the way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Three separate routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
The tower in front of the wall carries its own routes under a colliding name
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

FIRST, RULE OUT THE TOWER. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the OPEN WALL, and specifically on its CENTRE. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a SPECTACULAR CURVING CHIMNEY — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
The wall foreshortens badly from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate at the base
Same walk-off descent with a no-fall gap crossing near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached TOWER at the lower right of the wall; the deep GULLY between that tower and the mountain; and the OPEN CENTRE of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the CURVING CHIMNEY at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

NEGATIVE MARKER from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

approach_variants.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 11 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A full traverse of both Fury summits simply to reach the saddle
Glaciated terrain between Luna Col and the Fury summits
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no independent descent
Very little published route detail, and the peak itself is imprecisely located
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO NAMED SUMMITS AND YOU REACH IT BY HAVING CROSSED BOTH SUMMITS OF FURY. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. ARRIVAL: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the NORTHWEST ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. WHY THERE IS SO LITTLE HERE, SAID PLAINLY: Swiss Peak has one described route and no first-ascent record, the peak itself is not precisely located, and nothing published locates a feature at the foot of the southwest face. What is locatable is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col. WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

approach_variants.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length and is described only in outline, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A long off-trail ridge sequence with no maintained tread
No independent descent; exiting the range means committing to one of the long approach drainages
Very little published detail for either approach to this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PICKELL PASS THE SOUTH SIDE OF SWISS IS CLIMBED DIRECTLY, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE GOING UP RATHER THAN ALONG. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

HOW TO KNOW YOU ARE AT PICKELL PASS RATHER THAN ANOTHER SADDLE ON THE SAME RIDGE SYSTEM: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's NORTHEAST ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

WHY THIS SIDE MAY BE THE BETTER CHOICE, AS A PLANNING FACT RATHER THAN A LANDMARK: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

approach_variants.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
approach_variants.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the MOAT between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the SOUTH peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

approach_variants.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
approach_variants.notes:
FR 41 has washed out repeatedly and the closure point has moved. Reported blockages have been around five miles up from the Mountain Loop Highway, and at other times past the Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
approach_variants.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the SOUTH peak.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Okanogan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE EAST TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, north, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies north for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

approach_variants.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply RIGHT from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the NORTH side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct, snow-free
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and RIGHT of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, on snow
approach_variants.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Apr, ice and mixed
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.

approach_variants.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: There is no way to walk to this climb. Do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: No ground approach — a retreat means reversing or rappelling somebody else's route
Loose and deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Belays are bolted but not all of them are rigged for rappel, so this is not a line to bail down
Everything below you is occupied ground; manage rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are looking for a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge BELOW a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse LEFT along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

approach_variants.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it, and note that this is also the line most parties use to get back DOWN afterwards.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: No ground approach; escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose and deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rappel-rigged, so plan the descent before you leave the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material on it
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse LEFT — further than from the centre line — until you find the TWO-BOLT ANCHOR set on the ledge directly BELOW a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an UNBRIDGED FORD OF THE CHIWAWA RIVER, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A BROAD SADDLE ON THE SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, AND THE WAY YOU GET TO IT IS A SNOW FINGER RATHER THAN A SLOPE. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a SNOW FINGER AND ITS MOAT, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

THE SADDLE IS WHERE THE ROUTE LEAVES THE BASIN. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS PEAK AND IT IS ABOUT ASPECT: BERGE'S NORTH AND WEST FACES ARE CLIFFY. Parties must stay on the SOUTH-WEST side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE LOWER DOWN IS A DESCENDING TRAVERSE, WHICH FEELS WRONG AND IS RIGHT: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

THE LAST OBSTACLE HAS AN ELEVATION AND A CHARACTER: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with SLANTED SLABS and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

THE SUMMIT IS NOT ONE POINT. The TRUE, NORTH summit needs a short FOURTH-CLASS step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The EAST approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The NORTH approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour SOUTH under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH PASS APPROACH DELIVERS YOU TO THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN ON PURPOSE, AND THE RULE IS THAT YOU MUST KEEP GOING AROUND. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. THE CLIMB IS ON THE SOUTH-WEST SIDE. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

THE ARRIVAL IS THE SAME PLACE FOR EVERY APPROACH TO THIS PEAK: the broad SADDLE ON BERGE'S SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

THE APPROACH-SPECIFIC MARKER ON THE HIGH PASS LINE is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

THE 7,840 FT NOTCH IS THE LINK BETWEEN THE TWO SIDES and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

AND THE SAME SUMMIT WARNING APPLIES: the true summit is the NORTH one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-four miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Cornice at the top of the face — parties have had pieces release across their tracks
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse
Leroy Creek crossing running high in early season
Very poor rock quality throughout this group of peaks
Descending a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS NOT THE ROUTE, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go DOWN about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

THE TEST IS VISUAL AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: you have descended far enough when the face comes into FULL VIEW. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

WHAT NOT TO EXPECT: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the CORNICE at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay SOUTH and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side
A very long walk in on a trail that has burned in the past
Cornice at the top of the face
