approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its FOOT rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
approach_variants.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far LEFT until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite with a documented fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIFFS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO OVERSHOOT THEM BY 100 FT. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further LEFT past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT ONCE YOU ARE IN: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the FIRST CHOCKSTONE, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A SECOND chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

THE EXIT TEST FOR LATER: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn LEFT before the gully ends — look for TWO LARGE TREES and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

AND ONE DESCENT WARNING THAT PARTIES GET WRONG: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the MIDDLE summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

approach_variants.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall is very likely and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully — helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant rather than technical
Access: private property on the walking approach, closed to climbers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS THE OBVIOUS ONE ON THE SOUTH SIDE, AND THE TEST IS THAT IT FORCES YOU OUT LEFT. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE CHOCKSTONE, AND IT COMES EARLY. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' LEFT out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOURS: the big WEST face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col in a single push
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, roughly four miles east of Washington Pass and looking straight across the valley at Silver Star Mountain. There is no numbered Forest Service trail here — the whole thing is an established boot path.

Scramble down the embankment past cairns. The first stretch is loose, scree-covered talus before it settles into a proper path. Cross Early Winters Creek on one of the logs; the logjam shifts year to year, so look up and down stream for the best one, and expect a cold, pushy ford in early season.

On the far bank the path winds through forest for about a quarter of a mile, then turns straight uphill between two small creeks and climbs relentlessly. At about 6,460 ft the angle relents at a broad flat bench — big enough for a dozen tents and the obvious rest stop.

Above the bench the path climbs and traverses loose scree gullies before a final cairned stretch of very unstable scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. That is roughly 3,700 ft above the creek. That last scree is worse on the way down than the way up.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — logs shift, and the ford is cold and swift in early season
extremely unstable ball-bearing scree over slab on the final stretch to the col — this is the section that kicks rocks onto whoever is below, so travel close together
loose talus on the initial drop from the highway
very large gain for a day trip; most parties camp
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col is the destination and the route starts essentially straight off it. Burgundy Col is a narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and once you are stood in it the first pitch is directly above and visually obvious — the North Face rises immediately from the col rather than requiring any traverse along the base. If you have to walk any distance from the notch to find a start, you are at the wrong notch. Confirmation from the col: the Silver Star Glacier lies below on the far (east) side, so a col that drops onto a glacier behind you is the right one.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the 6,460 ft bench
approach_variants.notes:
The usual way this is done. Walk the same line from the milepost 166 pullout — down the loose talus embankment, across Early Winters Creek on logs, through the forest and then steeply up between the two small creeks — and stop at the broad flat bench at about 6,460 ft, which holds a dozen or more tents and is the natural halfway point. There is usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby.

Next morning you carry only what you need for the col and the route, which makes the loose scree above the bench substantially less unpleasant. Reckon on the bench being the last flat ground and the last water.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: the direct-looking gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
loose scree over slab on the traverse into the col
no water above the bench
rockfall onto parties below on the final approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, the route to the col climbs and traverses scree gullies with cairns on the final stretch. Aim for the narrow notch with Burgundy Spire on your left and Paisano Pinnacle on your right; the first pitch of the North Face rises directly out of it. Do not take the obvious direct gully that appears to lead straight to the col — it is loose and exposed. The path goes up the gully above camp and then makes a rising traverse right beneath the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: No climbers' trail to the base; navigation is off the landform and photographs
Long approach through burn with little shade and overgrown tread
A no-fall step-across or hop on the walk-off descent
Remote enough that a two- to four-day trip is the norm, so a retreat is slow
approach_variants.baseFinding: THERE IS NO CLIMBERS' TRAIL TO THE BASE. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the FIRST SWITCHBACK after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go UP INTO the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 FEET UP the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the LEFT wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a TALL PEDESTAL there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. HOW TO TELL THIS FROM THE SOUTH FACE ROUTES, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a TRAIL, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way OUT, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead with four different published names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up INTO the gully, and start on the LEFT wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRECT STARTS AT THE VERY BOTTOM OF THE ROCK, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE ROUTE IT SHARES A CAMP WITH. From the saddle you first go DOWN: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS LIES ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THAT ICE, WHERE THE ROCK RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW. THAT JUNCTION IS THE START. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: THE REGULAR NORTH BUTTRESS WALKS PAST THIS TOE AND CONTINUES UP THE GLACIER ON THE BUTTRESS'S CLIMBER'S-LEFT SIDE, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING ON SNOW WITH THE BUTTRESS RISING TO YOUR RIGHT, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE DIRECT AND ARE HEADING FOR THE REGULAR START. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A SECOND CHECK IS HOW SOON IT GETS HARD. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

WATCH THE MOAT AT THE JUNCTION. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, at the price of a legal border crossing on foot and an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, with passports
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL DIFFERS, THE START DOES NOT. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

TIE IN AT THE TOE OF THE ROCK ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE ICE, WHERE THE BUTTRESS RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW AND THERE IS NO MORE SNOW ABOVE YOU. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

approach_variants.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
approach_variants.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The notch is the low point on the skyline between Forbidden and Mount Torment, at 8,265 ft, and the couloir below it is the obvious continuous snow line splitting the left-hand edge of the south face. Navigate to the NOTCH, not to the first gully you reach — several lines start off the same snowfield and only this one tops out at the crest. You are at the base of the climbing when you step through the notch onto the ridge crest; from there the route to the summit runs to climber's right.

approach_variants.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
approach_variants.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cat Scratch is not the snow couloir, and that mix-up is the usual reason parties lose time here: it is the parallel ROCK gully system just west (climber's left) of the couloir, and it tops out at the same 8,265 ft notch. Several parallel gullies in that system look alike from below — the correct one finishes at the notch itself rather than on the ridge either side of it, so pick your line by where it ENDS on the skyline, not by which entrance looks easiest from the basin.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do NOT take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a FIRE-PIT CLEARING, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the DOWNSTREAM TIP OF A SMALL MID-CHANNEL ISLAND; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a BAND OF EXPOSED ROCK — stay RIGHT and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends LEFT up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the TALUS FAN toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for CANNOT BE SEEN FROM BELOW. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with TWO options off it, a left-hand line past a CHOCKSTONE that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered FROM the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

approach_variants.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
approach_variants.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented WRONG TURN in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
approach_variants.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the BOULDER at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LADDER OF LANDMARKS ABOVE THE BASIN IS WHAT FIXES YOUR POSITION, AND THEY COME IN ORDER. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - IF YOUR GULLY HAS NO CHOCKSTONE BOTTLENECK IN IT, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG DRAINAGE and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

FROM CAMP THE BASE OF THE ROUTE IS ANOTHER THOUSAND FEET OR SO ABOVE, GAINED ON SLABS AND CONNECTING GULLIES. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT IS ABOVE YOU. This route is on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the SOUTH of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

AND CHECK THAT YOU LEFT THE TRAIL AT ALL. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL CHANGES, THE APPROACH DOES NOT. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

THE MARKERS ARE THE SAME LADDER, IN THE SAME ORDER: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

THE SUMMIT TEST STILL APPLIES. This route is on the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TRAIL IS JUST BEYOND WILLOW LAKE, AND THE LAKE IS THE MARKER. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

FROM THERE THE GROUND IS THE TEST RATHER THAN ANY TREAD: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

ABOVE THE MEADOWS THE CLIFF BANDS ARE BYPASSED, NOT CLIMBED. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT DIRECTLY BENEATH THE BUTTRESS on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED SOMEWHERE WITH RUNNING WATER, YOU ARE NOT THERE YET. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek - reported both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge destroyed, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the start
crevasses and steep neve on the Jerry Glacier both ways
loose blocks on the crest - the rock on this mountain pulls off freely
sustained exposure with rappels needed to reverse the steps
a long committing position with a multi-hour retreat to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS THE CREST, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER LEAVE IT. From camp climb to the level step on the southeast ridge at about 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That step is the start: the ridge above it is the route, and everything you climb from there should have ground falling away on BOTH sides of you.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS HERE, BECAUSE THE WRONG TURN IS THE POPULAR ONE. From the same shoulder the South Face route turns WEST and makes a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, aiming for snow patches and a boulder with slings on it under a cliff band. IF YOU ARE WALKING SIDEWAYS ON SCREE WITH A WALL ABOVE YOU AND YOUR FEET IN A MOAT, YOU HAVE JOINED THE SOUTH FACE AND LEFT THIS ROUTE BEHIND. There is no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on the Direct.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND UNDER YOUR HANDS: the crest gives continuous scrambling with occasional steps rather than a traverse across a face, and the exposure is symmetrical. When the crest throws up a step you cannot scramble, the answer is a short pitch on the crest or a brief turn on its flank, not a traverse that takes you a rope length or more away from it.

A CROSS-CHECK HIGH ON THE ROUTE: near 8,600 ft the South Face rejoins the crest by way of a scree band beside a snow patch. If you are already on the crest well below that and stay on it, you and a South Face party will meet there having climbed two different mountains' worth of ground.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of the basin from the meadows camp
no water above the lakes or meadows
wind-exposed camps
loose ground on the climb back to the shoulder
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH CAMPS FEED THE SAME STARTING POINT - THE LEVEL STEP ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE BETWEEN ABOUT 7,000 AND 7,200 FT. From the lakes, cross the notch to the south and climb out of Crater Creek Basin to it; from the meadows, climb straight up to it.

RECOGNISE THE STEP BY THE GROUND GOING FLAT. The ridge eases into a level shoulder before rearing up again, and that flat is where the climbing starts. If the angle has not relented, you are still below it.

FROM THERE, STAY ON THE CREST. The moment the ground under you becomes a sidehill traverse on scree rather than a ridge with air on both sides, you have drifted onto the South Face's line beneath the cliff band. Turn back to the crest rather than continuing, because the two routes do not rejoin until near 8,600 ft.

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is NOT approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to roughly three quarters of an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the WEST side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Most parties instead rappel the East Face and return directly to their packs.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the talus, Liberty Crack is the obvious continuous vertical crack that passes to the RIGHT of the huge roof high on the wall — the roof is the Lithuanian Lip, and it is the single feature that identifies the line even in flat light. Do not scramble straight up beneath it. The standard entry traverses in from the LEFT for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to reach the ledges directly under the true first-pitch crack; there is also a fourth-class alternative that goes up the right-hand side of the block at the base. Parties that head straight up the fall line from the talus end up on the neighbouring East Face lines rather than on Liberty Crack — the East Face here holds a whole cluster of routes within a few rope lengths of each other, so pick the line by the roof above you, not by whichever crack is nearest.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
approach_variants.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identifier is still the big roof — Liberty Crack is the continuous crack running past the right side of the Lithuanian Lip. What changes is the last few metres: a deep moat opens where the snow pulls away from the base of the wall, and getting from snow into the rock can mean a committing step across or a short stemming move down and back up out of the gap. Scout along the base rather than dropping into the first moat you meet; parties have found the moat mellowing out within about thirty feet of where they first reached it.

approach_variants.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
hazards: wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun - axe, crampons if firm, early season
heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
no reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
the ridge is unsafe wet and unsafe without rock gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear RIGHT at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
hazards: exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
slide alder low down
no reliable water past the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PERFECT PASS IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BECAUSE THE GROUND STOPS AND THE GLACIER STARTS. From the pass, getting down onto the Challenger Glacier at about 7,000-7,200 ft can involve roughly 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The exact entry point moves year to year with crevasse conditions, so do not look for a particular spot; look for the lowest place you can step from rock onto continuous ice.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME THING AS ARRIVAL AT THE GLACIER: the technical climbing on this route is 50 ft long and it is the last 50 ft. Above the bergschrund the glacier steepens into a snow arete, then a clean 3rd-class scramble runs out at the base of a short, well-protected 5.5-5.7 pitch. THAT PITCH IS THE ROUTE. If you are roping up anywhere lower than the foot of a single unbroken 50 ft wall with a rappel anchor visible at its top, you have roped up too early.

THE MOAT IS THE MARKER YOU WILL MEET FIRST, AND IN FOG IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Just below the summit rocks a moat has been reported up to about 5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to hunt a snow bridge. Reaching an uncrossable gap where the snow has pulled away from the summit rock means you are at the base, not lost.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing east along the crest away from the summit block puts you on the connecting ridge toward Poltergeist Pinnacle and Crooked Thumb, which is a different day entirely.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE IMPASSE IS THE CHECKPOINT, NOT THE BASE, AND CONFUSING THE TWO IS THE COMMON ERROR IN CLOUD. It is a notch in the ridge guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 step to regain the crest beyond.

BEYOND IT, THE TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE OTHER APPROACH: Perfect Pass, then step onto ice, then keep going until the walking stops at a 50 ft rock wall. Nothing on this route is technical until that wall.

A NAMED WHITEOUT TRAP ON THIS LINE: on the snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, parties in fog have headed for Whatcom Peak's summit wall instead of the pass. If the ground in front of you is steepening into a wall rather than levelling into a saddle, you are aimed at the wrong feature. Perfect Pass is a saddle with running water; Whatcom's wall has neither.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail and Avalanche Canyon to the North Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Road-walk or bike about 5 miles up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at roughly 1,450 ft. The trail is unmaintained and gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — steep from the first half-mile, exposed roots and rock steps needing hands, no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a pack. Camp at the lake's north end.

From camp, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree and talus. Firm snow, when it is there, makes this whole section faster and safer than bare scree. This route does NOT take the South Chute: it stays in the canyon and climbs the North Chute higher up. Above the chute the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to reach the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Steep hard snow persists longer on the Terrible Traverse than on any other crux on this mountain, which is exactly the point of it
hazards: The Terrible Traverse crosses steep firm snow directly above a large cliff — an unprotected slip is very likely fatal
Hard, icy neve is common through June and early July; afternoon softening increases slip risk later in the day
Loose rock throughout the North Chute — classic Olympic choss, and rockfall from parties above is a real hazard
Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes, called out specifically for May-June conditions
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics, hard on the way down and slick when wet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS THE CAT EARS, AND FOR THIS ROUTE IT IS A NEGATIVE TEST — YOU WANT TO WALK PAST THEM. The Cat Ears are a rock tower standing just LEFT of the notch at the top of the South Chute, and the standard advice on the South Chute is to start climbing east out of the canyon as soon as the Cat Ears come into view. This route bypasses that. Keep going NORTH up Avalanche Canyon on loose talus, past the South Chute entrance, to the mouth of the North Chute further into the canyon. If you have turned east and are climbing toward a notch with a tower just left of it, you are in the South Chute and on the Finger Traverse route instead.

In cloud the Cat Ears are not visible and the discriminator becomes the canyon itself: the South Chute leaves the canyon EARLY and low; the North Chute is reached by staying in the canyon bed and continuing up it. When in doubt, keep walking up the canyon — the error that puts you on the wrong route is turning uphill too soon.

SECOND TEST, at the top of the chute: the Terrible Traverse is not the chute and it is not immediately above it. Above the North Chute the route LOSES a little elevation and traverses NORTH on ledges before it reaches the traverse at about 7,435 ft. If you have topped a chute and gone straight on up, you have not found it. The traverse itself is unmistakable when you arrive: a steep exposed snow crossing directly above a large cliff, or in late season a narrow rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above it. It is called the Terrible Traverse because a slip there does not stop.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: early to mid summer this is hard steep snow wanting an axe, crampons and, for many parties, pickets. Late season it often melts back to that rock ledge, which most parties find more secure. Neither is the wrong condition; they are different climbs.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long way in, and the one parties choose to avoid the Lake Constance trail. From the same Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Published trail mileages differ by several miles depending on where the count starts, so none is quoted. The upper stretch is open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass descend into UPPER Avalanche Canyon — which is where this variant differs usefully from the lake approach, because it puts you in the canyon ABOVE the lake rather than below it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow remnant below Crystal Pass is safe or gone
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and the descent into upper Avalanche Canyon is unmarked
Early-season snow remnant below Crystal Pass may want an axe and, for some parties, a rope
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt — carry it
All the Terrible Traverse hazards above, reached by a longer and more committing line
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COMING IN FROM CRYSTAL PASS YOU ENTER AVALANCHE CANYON FROM ABOVE, SO THE CAT EARS TEST RUNS BACKWARDS AND YOU MUST NOT LET IT PULL YOU DOWNHILL. Dropping south into the canyon from Crystal Pass you meet the North Chute's mouth FIRST and the South Chute entrance further down toward the lake. So the discriminator here is: the first chute you can turn up out of the canyon on the Constance side is the one you want. If you are still descending the canyon and have passed a chute on your left, you have gone below it.

THE FIXED LANDMARK THIS SIDE SHARES with the lake approach is the Cat Ears tower and the Thumb formation, both of which sit in the canyon between the two lines. Keep them BELOW you.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TEST IS THE SAME AS THE LAKE APPROACH: the route loses a little height and traverses NORTH on ledges to the base of the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft — a steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, or a narrow rock ledge in late season.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and lingering snow with real route-finding. This variant trades a brutal trail for a navigation problem; in cloud it is the harder of the two.

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
approach_variants.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Several little bowls look like the peak's south face and one of them is the wrong drainage entirely
A well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north — that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake, and the descent is the crux of the day
Loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever gully you pick through the cliff band
Slippery grass and dense alder low on the face when descending
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: MAKE SURE YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT DRAINAGE BEFORE YOU CLIMB — SEVERAL LITTLE BOWLS LOOK LIKE THIS FACE, AND THE ONE TO YOUR EAST IS ROYAL CREEK. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top. Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

approach_variants.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
approach_variants.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks near 6,500 ft and descend roughly nine hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: A substantial descent to Crescent Lake that must be reclimbed on the way out
Snow persisting on the col into late spring
Several little bowls look like the peak's south face — confirm the drainage before climbing
The same cliff band and loose, dirty Class 3 gullies above the lake
A long day made longer by the added distance and the col crossing
approach_variants.baseFinding: CRESCENT LAKE IS THE COMMON STARTING POINT, AND ON THIS SIDE YOU ARRIVE AT IT FROM ABOVE. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 11,000–11,100 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-right side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it
Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing
Avalanche, rockfall and steep snow in The Fan gully
Ice and rockfall raking the centre and east side of the Turtle snowfield
Thin or rotten ice in the chute late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts BELOW Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be LOSING height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: a first pitch of roughly 400 ft at 35–40 degrees on stepped ground that most parties climb with a single tool, then a second pitch of roughly 400 ft at 45–50 degrees where a second tool earns its place. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent — carry a saved track
Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail
Same serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then DOWN a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road
approach_variants.notes: Small pull-off at the old White Salmon lodge on the Mount Baker Highway. Walk around the gate and take the old road past the lodge site for about a mile until it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the glacier. Without good snow, do NOT go down into the valley — hold your height entering the clearcut and contour, shedding elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings. This is the same decision that governs the North Face approach, and it is the difference between a walk and a fight with slide alder. Going south past Lake Ann and over Austin Pass is not the way parties reach the White Salmon Glacier; the drainage is entered from the White Salmon side of the highway.
approach_variants.season: spring; snow cover strongly preferred
hazards: avalanche off the Hanging Glacier across the approach basin
brush in the valley bottom without snow cover
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
Winnie's Slide holds firm ice when it has melted back
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route proper begins at the foot of the White Salmon Glacier, or from the bivy sites up and right of it. Ascend the glacier weaving between rock outcrops and crevasses; the marker you are climbing toward is the base of Winnie's Slide at roughly 6,800 ft. Winnie's Slide is unmistakable once you are under it — the angle jumps to around forty to forty-five degrees for a few hundred feet, and it is the only thing on this side of the mountain that steepens like that. Above it you step onto the Upper Curtis Glacier.

If you are still on low-angle glacier threading around rock islands, you are below the slide, however long you have been walking. Conversely, if you have topped out on flatter glacier without a steep pitch behind you, you have drifted off the line and are somewhere else on the White Salmon.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: From the base of Chair 8, traverse downhill into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley and then climb over four thousand feet to near the base of Hell's Highway at the top of the glacier. This is the ski-descent party's usual line in.
approach_variants.season: winter/spring, on skis
hazards: a committing descent at the start that must be reclimbed on the way out
Hanging Glacier avalanche debris across the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: Winnie's Slide at about 6,800 ft is still the reference feature low on the route; higher, the head of the White Salmon is marked by the base of Hell's Highway. Neither is a subtle feature — both are abrupt steepenings out of low-angle glacier.

approach_variants.name: Duckabush River Trail to the unmarked creek turnoff
approach_variants.notes: Twenty-odd miles up the Duckabush over Big Hump, with a wide ford of the river above Duckabush Camp that runs thigh-deep and swift in early season. The climbers' line leaves the maintained trail roughly three miles below Marmot Lake. A multi-day backpack with a high camp at the lake or in the basin, never a car-to-car day.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
An unmarked turnoff and unmapped off-trail travel above the amphitheater
A wide river ford, worse in the afternoon than at dawn
Fallen timber through the burned sections of the lower valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: The turnoff is unmarked — no sign, cairns at best — and getting it right is the whole navigation problem on this route. Above Duckabush Camp, watch for a small feeder creek coming in from climber's-left and follow it up out of the valley. It leads into a rocky amphitheater on the west side of the summit, and that amphitheater is the base: once you are standing in it the climbing is easy Class 2 heather and talus straight up to the summit ridge, so the hard part is behind you. The maintained trail runs on past the turnoff toward the pass, so if you find yourself gaining the pass or arriving at Marmot Lake you have walked past the creek and should drop back down the trail. Snow fills the amphitheater and the slopes above into summer and cornices build on the summit ridge into late June, so carry an axe and treat the crest as possibly unsupported. Water is dependable at the creek and scarce once you leave it — fill up before you start climbing.

approach_variants.name: First Divide and the unnamed lake basin
approach_variants.notes: Parties generally find this the easier of the two lines and it is much shorter, but the corridor on that side has been closed by fire damage — confirm before planning around it. From the divide the route runs west into a basin, then over a col and north along the crest.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Cornices and unconsolidated snow on the summit ridge into late June
Avalanche potential on east-facing slopes below the summit early season
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall on the closed valley corridor
Open ground above the basin that is easy to lose in fog
Loose talus on the connecting slopes either side of the col
approach_variants.baseFinding: From First Divide, follow the ridge west into a basin holding an unnamed lake. That lake is the marker for this whole variant — it is the only standing water in the basin and it sits directly below the two summit humps of Steel, so if you are in an open basin with no lake in it you are in the wrong one. From the lake, drop southwest to the saddle between those humps; the saddle is the base of the climb, and from it you turn north along the summit ridge for the final easy Class 2 stretch to the high point. The direction of that turn is the thing to get right. Duckabush lies beyond the same col to the southwest and reads as the higher, more striking mountain from below, so a party that turns the wrong way off the saddle ends up committed to a different peak. The early-summer cornice and unconsolidated-snow caution applies just as strongly on this side: the crest holds snow late and it is not always attached to the rock beneath it, so stay back from the eastern lip.

approach_variants.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the COMPLETE North Ridge, which begins at about 6,700 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to NOT mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

approach_variants.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.
