About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through the summer
~2,000 ft of descent on the way in, all of which must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass
Approach consistently underestimated; parties arrive at the toe late and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the WEST, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,700 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

approach_variants.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp, then turn up at the Brush Creek Trail junction and climb through US Cabin Camp, Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. A cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack exists near U.S. Cabin Camp as an alternative to fording. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack, which reports rate as the riskier option
An unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BROAD TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND YOU FIND IT BY WALKING SOUTH OFF THE PASS UNTIL THE PATH DIES. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads DIRECTLY SOUTH, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is STAY ON THE CREST rather than follow any marked line.

SO THE FOG TEST IS A HANDRAIL TEST, AND IT IS THE BEST KIND: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

ARRIVAL AT THE START: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

WHAT THE UPPER RIDGE IS LIKE, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER YOU COME BACK THIS WAY: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

AND THE OTHER THING THIS RIDGE IS: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told NOT to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

approach_variants.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
The same loose upper ridge as the western approach
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER WAY YOU ARRIVE AT WHATCOM PASS, THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL: leave the maintained trail, head DIRECTLY SOUTH on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

THE ONE THING THIS SIDE CHANGES, AND IT IS A LOGISTICS FACT RATHER THAN A NAVIGATION ONE: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE PASS AND NOT AT A CAMP BELOW IT: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.

approach_variants.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs just under four miles and roughly two thousand two hundred feet to the lake. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE LEAVES THE TRAIL AT THE LAKE - THERE IS NO TREAD BEYOND IT. From the lake basin the south-east ridge rises to the north-west toward a col at about 8,000 ft. THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND THE TEST IS SYMMETRY: once established you should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

IF THE GROUND CLOSES IN AND YOU ARE CLIMBING A CONFINED, EXTREMELY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE SLIPPED OFF THE CREST ONTO A FLANKING GULLY. Those gullies are the other route's ground, gained from the next drainage north, and they are notably worse rock than the crest.

AT THE COL NEAR 8,000 FT THE SUMMIT IS ALONG THE CREST, NOT DIRECTLY ABOVE. A SMALL SEPARATE PEAK STANDS WEST OF THE RIDGE SADDLE AND IS ROUTINELY MISTAKEN FOR THE TOP; the true high point is the EASTERN one and reaching it is a tedious traverse over talus and large boulders past several intervening bumps.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS EFFORT, NOT ELEVATION: if you arrived at a summit within a few minutes of gaining the crest and did not cross bouldery bumps to get there, you are on the wrong high point and should look east along the ridge.

approach_variants.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
approach_variants.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE CREST IS GAINED BY A LOOSE GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS UNPLEASANT ENOUGH THAT ITS QUALITY IS THE CONFIRMATION. Parties commonly exit it about half-way up onto the parallel rib, which holds more solid rock, and return to it higher; the rib is a refuge beside the gully rather than a separate line, so keep the gully in sight.

IF THE CHUTE YOU ARE IN IS SOLID AND ENJOYABLE, IT IS PROBABLY NOT THE ONE - several chutes rise out of this basin and the route's own is notorious.

AT THE TOP THE SADDLE IS ON THE CREST, AND THE SUMMIT IS EAST OF IT. A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE; a summit reached in a few minutes by turning left out of the gully is that lower point, not the top.

THE TRUE HIGH POINT COSTS A TRAVERSE over talus and large boulders past intervening bumps. Arriving without that traverse means you are in the wrong place. Coming from this side the ridge is joined further west than the south-east ridge joins it, which is exactly why this mistake is easier to make on this approach than on the other one.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops BELOW the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the FAR side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy RAMP about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
approach_variants.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.

approach_variants.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HARDEST THING TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH IS THE PATH ITSELF, AND IT IS FOUND AT A FIREPIT. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ENDS at a small clearing with an old firepit. THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES ON THE LEFT NEAR THAT CLEARING, unsigned and steep from its first step. FIX THE SPOT IN YOUR MIND ON THE WAY IN - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

THE SECOND DECISION IS A CAIRNED FORK NEAR 5,200 FT. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; STAY RIGHT AND UPHILL ON THE CLIMBERS' PATH. IF YOU ARE LOSING HEIGHT TOWARD WATER, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE FISHERMAN'S TRAIL.

EXPECT TO LOSE THE TREAD ON THE RIDGE AND NOT TO PANIC ABOUT IT. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. WHEN IN DOUBT, STAY ON THE CREST.

THE CLIMB PROPER STARTS ABOVE THE LAKE MEADOWS. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A ROCK WALL LINES THE EAST SIDE OF THAT OUTLET; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

ROPE UP BEFORE STEPPING ONTO THE SNOW, NOT PART-WAY ACROSS. IF YOU ARE TRYING TO CLIMB A ROCK WALL BESIDE THE OUTLET STREAM, YOU HAVE MISSED THE TURN AROUND ITS END.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
approach_variants.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE CLIMB STARTS AT THE HEAD OF THE LAKE'S OUTLET STREAM. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A ROCK WALL RUNS ALONG THE EAST SIDE OF IT - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of that wall with a single class 3 step. FORCING THE WALL DIRECTLY IS THE WRONG ANSWER AND IS HOW PARTIES GET STOPPED HERE.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE NOTCH, NOT THE ANGLE. You should step DOWN into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the LEFT, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 8-9 hours and 12-13 miles in for a strong party. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE CAMP ENDS: FROM PERFECT PASS, HEAD NORTH AND UP ONTO THE BROAD SOUTH SNOWFIELD. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a CONSPICUOUS COL IN THE SUMMIT RIDGE above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

SO THE AIMING POINT IS A NOTCH IN A SKYLINE, AND IN CLOUD THE SUBSTITUTE FOR IT IS THIS: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow RUNS OUT AGAINST ROCK. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

CONFIRM ABOVE: the final stretch along the crest is SHORT, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

THE VARIATION THAT IS NOT AN ERROR: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the NORTHEAST of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

THE IMPASSE, WHICH IS THE OTHER THING YOU HAVE TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.

approach_variants.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
approach_variants.notes: An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT IS DEFINED BY WHAT IT AVOIDS, AND THAT IS THE TEST: IF YOU HAVE CROSSED THE IMPASSE, YOU ARE NOT ON IT. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

ARRIVAL IS THE SAME ARRIVAL: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

WHAT YOU TRADE FOR IT, AND WHY THE CHOICE IS A CONDITIONS CALL RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the WHATCOM GLACIER, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
approach_variants.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base of the actual climb when the climbers' path fades out in a large meandering gully at the bottom of a broad debris and deposition fan, with the couloir narrowing above it — roughly 4,000-4,300 ft. The path ending is the marker; there is no cairn or sign.

Above that, two features tell you the route is going right.

The Hourglass, near 5,800 ft, is a narrow rock and snow constriction and the crux of getting to the summit block: a couple of exposed 3rd-to-4th class moves in summer, or a steep 35-45 degree snow neck in spring which can be a thin snow bridge and which opens a moat at its base as it melts.

Higher, at the top of the snow, there is a notch with a large rock in it. Climb AROUND that rock to the RIGHT to reach the scree gully beyond. The general rule reported by parties who lose the thread here is: when in doubt, go right.

Cairns exist most of the way, but several of them are misleading. Treat a cairn as a hint and the terrain as the authority. The final roughly 200 vertical feet to the true south summit is class 4 with real exposure.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow ascent
approach_variants.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
approach_variants.season: Apr-May, snow
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The deposition fan at the foot of the couloir is still the mark, but under snow the fan and the couloir merge visually. Read it by width: the base is where the open fan narrows into a defined couloir line, several hundred feet of which you then climb before exiting onto its west side and continuing up toward the spur.

The Hourglass around 5,800 ft is the feature to inspect from below. In spring it is a steep snow neck at 35-45 degrees and is sometimes a thin snow bridge — a moat at its base is the sign it is going.

The notch with the large rock at the top of the snow is still passed on the RIGHT.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
approach_variants.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIR IS VISIBLE FROM THE LAKE AND THAT IS THE POINT OF APPROACHING FROM THIS SIDE. From the water, look south-west at the peak: THE ROUTE IS THE OBVIOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE THAT SPLITS THE SUMMIT BLOCK ITSELF. Pick it out before you start moving, because from underneath the flanking gullies all look alike.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHERE THE LINE ENDS. IT MUST TOP OUT ON THE SUMMIT BLOCK, NOT ON THE RIDGE BESIDE IT. A couloir that finishes at a notch with more mountain above it and to one side is one of the flanking gullies and not the route.

THE SECOND TEST IS ASPECT. This is the NORTH side: it should be the shaded flank, holding firmer snow than anything around it in the morning and going soft late. IF THE SNOW YOU ARE STANDING ON IS IN EARLY SUN, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO AN EASTERN OR WESTERN FLANK.

THE THIRD TEST IS CONTINUITY. The route is a single continuous line from the basin to the top of the block. If the snow you are following breaks into disconnected patches with rock steps between them, you are either too late in the season for it or on a different feature.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN. There is a similarly named peak elsewhere in the range that is reached from an entirely different valley and has nothing to do with this one. The confirmation here is that the lake lies immediately north-east of your peak and the summit stands directly across it from you.

approach_variants.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
approach_variants.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIXED POINT ON THIS SIDE IS THE LAKE, AND EVERYTHING ABOVE IT IS READ OFF THE PEAK ITSELF. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the mountain stands to the south-west and the route faces you.

THE ROUTE IS THE CONTINUOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE CLEAVING THE SUMMIT BLOCK. It must finish ON the block. A gully that tops out on the ridge to either side of the summit is a flanking line, not the route.

USE SHADE AS THE CONFIRMATION: the north side holds shadow while the basin around it is lit, and the snow in it stays firm longest in the morning.

BECAUSE THE APPROACH FROM THIS SIDE IS UNMARKED, FIX YOUR LINE INTO THE BASIN ON THE WAY IN. There is no tread to follow back out, and the basin has no obvious exit when seen from above.

approach_variants.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
approach_variants.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lone Tree Pass CANNOT be picked out from directly beneath it, and that is the single most useful thing to know about this approach. Look at the mountain from the valley before you start — from the highway at Darrington — and fix where the pass sits relative to the shoulder, because once you are traversing inside the forest between 4,500 and 4,700 ft there is nothing to aim at. The confirmation from inside the trees is the ground itself: you are traversing, not climbing, and the correct entry is where that traversing forest opens into a BROAD snow couloir. A narrow gully or a steep timbered rib is not it.

For the upper half, the landmark is White Benchmark, Point 6357 — a blocky tower that works as a lighthouse for the whole rising traverse to High Pass. Keep it in view and aim at it; the broad gully up to the pass is right there. If you have run out of the rising traverse without a blocky tower above you, you are low and short of the pass.

The climbing itself starts at High Pass, where you cross onto the glacier. Snow travel of up to about thirty-five degrees leads to the summit snow ridge. The final marker is at the very top: by midsummer the bergschrund and moat below the summit rock often force a short section of fifth-class rock or a delicate roped step across a snow bridge, so the route does not simply walk out on snow.

approach_variants.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
approach_variants.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
approach_variants.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window
approach_variants.baseFinding: This variation rejoins the same upper ground, so the markers are unchanged: White Benchmark (Point 6357) for the traverse to High Pass, and High Pass itself as the step onto the glacier. The specific trap here is timing rather than terrain — if you are fighting slide alder rather than walking on snow, the line is out of condition and the standard Niederprum trail is the better choice that day.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route walk-in, which is why the two are so often climbed on the same day. Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass; a mile and a half of maintained trail to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream, marked with a large cairn; then the climbers' path up slabs, talus and heather into the bowl below the towers and up the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft.

In the gully, staying climber's left for the lower two thirds and then crossing to climber's right keeps you on the most stable ground.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose, heavily trafficked gully below the notch — helmets, and don't queue underneath another party
hollow-sounding flakes on the upper pitches send debris to the notch
no water above the stream at the Trail #727 junction
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route starts AT the top of the notch, on the Concord (south) side — not below it. Stand on the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord col and turn to face Concord Tower: the first pitch is the crack system running up that wall to a large ledge holding a few small trees, and that ledge is the pitch-one belay and is visible from the notch. The mistake to avoid is dropping 30 feet down the Liberty Bell side to the tree with the ledge running left into a blocky chimney — that is the Beckey Route on Liberty Bell, the other tower, and parties heading for opposite summits share this saddle all day. If your first pitch tops out on a treed ledge you are on Concord; if it starts by walking a small ledge leftward into a chimney you are on Liberty Bell.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, but the gully feeding the Liberty Bell-Concord notch holds snow into late June most years and the boot path lower down may still be buried. Ice axe standard, crampons if it has refrozen.

One upside of the early season here: while the gully is snow-filled the rock in it is locked in place, and rockfall gets noticeably worse once it melts out.

SR-20 is closed across Washington Pass every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so this window begins whenever the highway reopens.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through late Jun
hazards: firm snow in the gully with a long runout below
moat between snow and rock at the base
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access until the highway reopens
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the start — it is still the crack system on the Concord wall rising directly from the crest of the notch to the treed ledge. What snow does is fill the notch, so the col reads as a smooth saddle and the base of the first pitch can sit above a moat. Look up at the tower on the south side of the col for the treed ledge to confirm you are on the right wall before committing.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited May 1 to September 30.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS CLIMB IS A FORK, AND THE FORK IS MARKED BY A ROCK FORMATION CALLED THE THUMB. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to MOUNT Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to INNER Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

THE FOG TEST THAT DOES NOT NEED THE THUMB, AND IT IS THE BETTER ONE, IS THE SHAPE OF THE GULLY YOU END UP IN. From the broad couloir, veer RIGHT into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled DEFILE. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

SECOND TEST, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE RECORDED WAY THIS ROUTE GOES WRONG: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which has no easy connection across to the true NORTHEAST high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

SAFETY NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE ROUTE-FINDING: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CRYSTAL PASS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS DIRECTLY BELOW YOU RATHER THAN ABOVE YOU, WHICH IS THE ONE REAL ADVANTAGE OF THIS SIDE. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the RIGHT (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

THE TEST IS STILL THE THUMB AND THE DEFILE, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the RIGHT side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

THE FOG TEST FOR THAT NORTHEAST LINE IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON. Stay on the crest's RIGHT-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the NORTHEAST top.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.notes: READ THE NAME ON THIS ROUTE WITH CARE — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies WEST of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin, and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond the basin
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August, over a buried climbers' path
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and along the ridge connecting the three summits
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Obstruction Point Road closes for most of the year and is not a route you can count on before July
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS CAMERON PASS AND THE TEST IS THE DIRECTION YOU TURN OUT OF IT: THE RIDGE YOU CLIMB RISES TO THE EAST. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. SECOND TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE: THE RIDGE IS A SEQUENCE OF FALSE SUMMITS. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going until a short Class 3-4 section leads to the top — that step is the deciding feature of the peak. THIRD TEST, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. HONEST LIMIT AND A LIVE DISAGREEMENT: this route's own summit waypoint calls the EAST Peak the true 7,190 ft high point, while traverse accounts reach the true summit FIRST from Cameron Pass and then go on to Middle and East. Those cannot both be right. Carry a map, count your summits, and do not treat either the route title or the waypoint name as settled.

approach_variants.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
approach_variants.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant, reached after a longer approach
Bear canister required; no reliable water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE AT CAMERON PASS: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP, over many false summits, until a short Class 3-4 step leads to the top. The pass is WEST of the summit whatever the route title says. THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
approach_variants.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles at a washout about a mile in since 2002. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Many extra miles including a long closed-road walk at each end
A multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant
approach_variants.baseFinding: IDENTICAL AT THE PASS: the ridge rises EAST out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, to a short Class 3-4 step and the true top. THE TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS IS ABOUT WHICH VALLEY YOU ARE IN, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first. HONEST LIMIT: this approach is not the one the trailhead record names.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet, self-issue Olympic National Park wilderness permit at the kiosk — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. The Maynard Burn Trail continues straight and is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp at about 3.4 miles is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The notch below the divide holds 35-40 degree snow and an axe is worth carrying outside late season
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow basalt that breaks away readily, with rockfall funnelled by the gullies above the col
A Class 4 step on poor rock over steep runout dirt that must be reversed on descent — one party graded a move on the downclimb at 5.8
A reported moat over 30 ft deep below the gully late in the season
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer, and a 35-40 degree snow slope below the Royal-Deception notch
Remote terrain — a solo traveller died in a fall near the peak's south end in July 2022
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE LOWER LEFT CORNER OF THE MYSTERY GLACIER, AND THE THING THAT MARKS IT IS A LAKE YOU CANNOT MISTAKE FOR ANYTHING ELSE: A JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE SITS AT THE GLACIER'S BASE. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its LOWER LEFT corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

THE TEST FOR THE GLACIER CROSSING IS A DIAGONAL: you enter at the lower LEFT and exit at the upper RIGHT, at a COL at about 6,700 ft on the peak's EAST side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

SECOND TEST, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach OPEN SNOW ABOUT 200 FT SOUTH OF THE COL, then climb those slopes STAYING SOUTH OF the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

THIRD TEST, and it is the commitment point: a short CLASS 4 STEP on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a NOTCH NEAR 7,500 FT. Trend CLIMBER'S LEFT on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

WHAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE THROUGH: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and THE ROCK GETS MARKEDLY BETTER than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.

approach_variants.name: Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
approach_variants.notes:
The other side, and the one that suits a party already camped at Home Lake for Fricaba or Warrior. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, Trail #833.2 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Shelter at about 6.4 miles and 4,890 ft, then the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake at roughly 9.3 miles and 5,308-5,330 ft. From camp, climbers' paths lead up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, and from there the route traverses and descends west into upper Deception Basin.

This is the same basin the Royal Basin parties drop into, reached from the opposite end. It is the approach a high-route party is already on, and one detailed account describes exiting this way over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips and Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels — a valid variant exit, distinct from reversing the ascent.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose scree traverses between Constance Pass and Deception Basin
All the summit-block hazards of the standard variant, including the reversible Class 4 step
Steep snow lingering on the Constance Pass and Deception Basin traverse into July
Long committing backcountry travel far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE IN DECEPTION BASIN, and the shared test is the good one: the JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE at the foot of the Mystery Glacier. Get on the ice at its LOWER LEFT corner and cross diagonally to the COL AT ABOUT 6,700 FT at its UPPER RIGHT, on the peak's EAST side.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Constance Pass, because you arrive at Deception Basin along its length rather than dropping into its head. Leave the maintained trail at the pass and work WEST and DOWN into the upper basin. Loose scree on the descent is normal here. If you are contouring without losing height you have not committed to the basin; if you are climbing again you have crossed it and are heading for the Fricaba-Hal Foss ridge instead.

ABOVE THE COL THE TESTS ARE THE SAME: open snow about 200 ft SOUTH of the col, climbed staying SOUTH of the blocky rock band; then a short Class 4 step approached CLIMBER'S LEFT to a notch near 7,500 ft; then a clean Class 3 gully on markedly better rock to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS A SADDLE INSIDE THE BUTTRESS, AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND YOU GET THERE BY LOSING HEIGHT FIRST. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 FT DESCENDING TRAVERSE EAST across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft WITHIN the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

SO THE TEST IN CLOUD IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND, NOT THE VIEW: you go DOWN and EAST for a thousand feet, then UP a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes: The line the recorded distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 14 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IN THIS DRAINAGE THE NAVIGATION RULE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THING THAT MAKES THE DAY WORK. The creek must be forded in places, and FORDS GET HARDER THE LOWER AND FARTHER DOWNSTREAM YOU ARE. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

ARRIVAL, WHICH IS UNAMBIGUOUS EVEN WITH NO VISIBILITY: above the brush line the drainage OPENS into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

FROM THERE THE BASE TEST IS THE SAME ONE THE NORTHERN APPROACH USES: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A REAL RISK PECULIAR TO THIS APPROACH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT HAS HAPPENED: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek. Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp. From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock. The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at an entry on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Early season the moat at the toe is filled and the walk-in is snow; late season the moat opens and the last few metres onto rock can be the awkward part of the day
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
KEEP THE ICE CLIFF GLACIER ON YOUR LEFT AND WALK UNTIL THE ROCK STOPS YOU. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a BIG LEDGE about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the SOUTH side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse EAST below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY ABOVE THE MORAINE MOUND AND KEEP TRAVERSING. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking DOWN onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

ARRIVAL: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered eight or nine miles and about 4,500 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the WEST side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS A SEPARATE OBJECT AND THE PLATEAU IS NOT THE TOP. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct BLOCK that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

SO THE TEST IS: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the WESTERN slopes to the foot of the block.

WHICH SIDE OF THE BLOCK, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS IN CLOUD: the way up is a RAMP on the block's SOUTH side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

WHAT THE RIGHT GROUND FEELS LIKE: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

STAGING CHECK BELOW THE PLATEAU: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their WEST side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH APPROACHES CONVERGE ON THE DRUID PLATEAU, SO THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS NOT. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are NOT on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

WHAT STILL HOLDS: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its WESTERN slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its SOUTH side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

THE NORTH-SIDE-SPECIFIC WARNING: the ground below the basin has CLIFF BANDS in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

AND A ROUTE-CHOICE NOTE: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
approach_variants.notes:
