Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are TWO trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads NORTH. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading WEST, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn LEFT, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the LEFT path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The handrail is elevation plus one named feature. Follow the scramble gully on the RIGHT side of the rounded spur upward until the spur runs into the summit formation at about 6,400 ft. That contact point — where broken spur ground ends against continuous rock — is where the approach stops and the climb starts.

From there the line is the obvious gully on the upper LEFT, to the left of the South Buttress. If the buttress is on your left you have gone too far right; the buttress should be to your RIGHT as you enter the gully.

One recorded refinement inside that gully, which is around a hundred yards long: stay right at first and cross left higher up, scrambling on rock, rather than taking the centre — the middle holds the loose rock and the steeper steps.

One to two pitches of the southwest face above the gully reach the ridge crest, and most parties rope up for that even though it is graded fourth class. From the crest it is a short scramble to the top.

What is NOT here, and the absence is worth saying: there is no famous single wrong gully at Cathedral Rock. The published hazard is rockfall and loose rock, stated repeatedly and in plain terms. The genuinely wrong-start stories on this peak are all from the Northeast Buttress, a different route on the other side, so do not import them.

approach_variants.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
approach_variants.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pond you gain the same summit gully, but from below and on the south side rather than by traversing in from the pass. Climb to the ledge above the pond and follow it to the foot of the gully system.

The identification is unchanged: you want the gully to the LEFT of the South Buttress, entered where the spur ground dies against the continuous summit rock near 6,400 ft. Coming from the pond you meet that rock from underneath, so the check is that the buttress stands to your right as you turn up into the gully.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Spider Gap (standard)
approach_variants.notes: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (~3,500 ft), Trail #1511 climbs the valley about 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows, then into upper Phelps Basin and up the Spider Glacier snowfield to Spider Gap at 7,100 ft. Descend the north side — the steepest 100 vertical feet first, softer snow tends to be climber's-left — then scree and easing snowfield past the Lyman Glacier to Lower Lyman Lake, and back up about 1.8 miles of open meadow to Cloudy Pass at 6,438 ft. This is the line the recorded distance matches.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep
hazards: Spider Gap is the crux of the approach — a permanent snow/glacier slope that is a straightforward boot-pack in summer but can hold open crevasses and firm icy snow early season. Carry an axe and know how to use it.
A whiteout or an early-morning refreeze moves crampons from optional to necessary.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cloudy Pass is the staging point, not the base: the climbing starts where the boot path leaves the meadows and gains the southwest ridge, with the summit about 1,500 ft above the pass.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail from Trinity, over Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative reaching Cloudy Pass from the Trinity Trailhead by way of Buck Creek Pass. One of the three ways in; it is a multi-day trip rather than a variation on the standard day.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek from Holden Village
approach_variants.notes: Reaches Lower Lyman Lake and Cloudy Pass from Holden Village, which is itself reached by the Lake Chelan boat and a vehicle shuttle. The longest of the three and the one with the most fixed logistics.
approach_variants.season: Jul–Sep

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with CAIRNS and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately NORTH of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is CORRECT and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
approach_variants.notes:
White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft — subject to the same long-running road access problems as the Sitkum approach, so confirm before relying on it. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT about three miles — roughly two thirds of a mile past the Kennedy Creek crossing, which is your water — to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: long-running road access problems on the White Chuck side
unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. THAT saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are NOT visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

approach_variants.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
very long PCT approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the Kennedy Ridge variation
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
approach_variants.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: twenty-mile-plus approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the other variations
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

approach_variants.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir
approach_variants.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Two cliffbands in steep timber with no marked line through them
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir — helmets, and a tight party
Crevasses and moats on the Hagan Glacier ice apron even in summer
The descent reverses ground that reads very differently from above
approach_variants.baseFinding: A BROAD SCREE-AND-TALUS COULOIR, TOPPING OUT AT A COL AT THE SOUTHWEST END OF THE CRAGS. From the open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank, one broad couloir of loose scree and talus leads up to a col near the SOUTHWEST end of the line of Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. That col is the base of the climbing, and the slabs above it on the south side go at Class 3 to the top. Hagan is a massif of several crags rather than a single peak, so which col you reach matters: if the notch you have gained sits in the middle of the crags with towers rising on both sides of you, it is not this one — keep working to the southwest end of the line. Note carefully where the couloir meets the heather benches before you leave them, because it is also the way down and it is far harder to identify from above.

approach_variants.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
approach_variants.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard between lower Blum Lake and the pass
The Blum climbers' path is faint, brushy and marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif — easy to commit to the wrong summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE PASS SITS BETWEEN THE SOUTH AND MIDDLE PEAKS, AND IT IS THE SOUTH PEAK YOU CLIMB. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's NORTH side to a notch on its UPPER EAST side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead (about 4,240 ft) at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, FR 9737. A free self-issue Alpine Lakes wilderness permit is filled out at the register.

There are TWO forks and they are easily run together. The first comes at roughly a quarter to half a mile, where the old mine-road grade splits: bear RIGHT onto Ingalls Way #1390. Straight on is Esmeralda Basin #1394, a different valley. The second fork is higher, around 5,600 ft and roughly a mile and a half in: RIGHT climbs to Longs Pass, which is a viewpoint and the way toward Ingalls Creek and Stuart's south side, not a way to this climb. Stay LEFT.

From there the trail traverses steadily to Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group come into view all at once. Continue about another mile to Lake Ingalls, roughly 6,400-6,480 ft and about 4 miles from the car. This is the last water.

From the lake, work up and climber's-left on Class 2-3 slabs, talus and boulders. Stay with the cairned line. Parties who leave it for a more direct-looking line get cliffed out; one party downclimbed past a waterfall to escape.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the slabs above the lake are clear; snow lingers below the notch into early summer
hazards: Cliffing out on the slabs above and beside the lake if you leave the cairned line for a direct one
Loose talus and scree in the approach gully with parties above
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed ridge — start early
A 60 m rope does not reach on the descent rappels, roughly fifteen feet short; carry a 70 m or doubles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is visible from the lakeshore: the cleft between the North and South peaks, with a single pointed spire sitting in it. That spire is the Dogtooth. Aim just left of it and let it draw you up the slabs.

At the Dogtooth, go RIGHT for the traditional approach gully. The last gully is scree. If the gully you are in is green and lush it is the wrong one and it will carry you too high — traverse right out of it onto clean scree.

Arrival is physical: a short section of Class 4 up a crack of roughly forty feet at the top of the gully lands you on a ledge. That ledge is where the rope comes out. Pitch one is the low-angle slab above it, taking the large crack system up the middle.

Touch test at the start: the rock here is green serpentine, an odd slick band quite unlike the surrounding granite, sitting just up from the Dogtooth crag. Large hexes work in it where cams skate. Confirmation higher up — the pitch-three ledge carries two big bolts and there are three more at the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this is the one that matters. This route climbs the south ridge of the NORTH peak, and the North peak (7,662 ft) is the true summit. The South peak (7,640 ft) is a separate Class 3 scramble that starts from the SAME notch. If you reached the notch, dropped about fifty feet down its west side and scrambled easy gullies back to a top without ever roping up, you climbed the South peak. That is not this route and not the high point.

Second marker: finishing the technical pitches does not put you on the summit. There is a few hundred feet of walking left to tag the actual high point, so a summit that arrives the instant the climbing ends is the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Ingalls Pass. Just past the pass the trail splits and the right-hand branch is signed Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2. It drops into Headlight Basin, crosses Headlight Creek, and holds the established campsites and the reliable water. The main #1390 stays high along the rim of the basin and is the more direct line to the lake.

The two rejoin at a signed junction less than a quarter mile below Lake Ingalls, so this costs you a descent and a re-ascent in exchange for a legal camp and running water. Parties climbing the same day generally take the high line; parties camping take the low one.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this is the branch to take if you are sleeping out, since camping at Lake Ingalls is prohibited
hazards: Headlight Creek crossing
Braided use paths through the basin camps — stay on durable ground, this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness
Extra descent and re-ascent on the way out with a full pack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This branch does not change where the climbing starts — it rejoins the standard line at the signed junction below the lake, and from there the Dogtooth, the scree gully and the forty-foot Class 4 crack onto the belay ledge are exactly as on the high route.

What it does change is your starting view. Coming up out of Headlight Basin you meet the lake from below rather than from the pass, so you will not have had the long look across at the peak that the high traverse gives you. Walk to the lake outlet and pick out the notch and the Dogtooth spire from there before starting up the slabs, rather than trying to identify them mid-scramble.

approach_variants.name: Blanca Lake Trail to Virgin Lake, then the south-ridge climbers' path
approach_variants.notes: From the Blanca Lake trailhead at the end of the North Fork road, follow the lake trail north into the wilderness. It climbs immediately in a long series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining most of the day's easy elevation over the first three miles to a ridge crest — muddy, rooty and icy in wet or early-season conditions. From the ridge the trail DROPS about six hundred feet to Virgin Lake, a good overnight camp and the last easy reliable water before the off-trail climbing. This is where the single most common navigation error happens.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Early season adds snow on the ridge and makes the glacier variant the safer of the two.
hazards: The unsigned turnoff at Virgin Lake is the commonest error on this peak
Route-finding on the faint ridge path, which is easy to lose in brush
Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block with real exposure
Dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse late in the season
A long single push with a likely after-dark return unless camped at the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: At Virgin Lake, do NOT continue downhill on the main tread — that goes to the big turquoise lake below and away from the peak. Instead pick up the faint, UNSIGNED climbers' path leaving the lake into the woods toward the ridge. It gains the peak's south ridge and follows it northeast, staying on the ridge's EAST side to get round minor gendarmes, levels out around fifty-three hundred feet, crosses to the WEST side around fifty-eight hundred, then climbs steep heather and scree working around cliff bands. The technical ground starts at a NOTCH beside a subsidiary point, reached across a boulder field — the notch is the first place the ridge is blocked by a rock step you cannot walk around, and above it the rock turns loose and pebbly for the scramble to the summit ridge. Negative markers: if you are on obvious maintained tread descending toward a turquoise, silty lake, you took the main trail at Virgin Lake and are heading away from the peak; if you are roped up on a glacier, you are on the alternative line rather than this one.

approach_variants.name: Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake basin
approach_variants.notes: The alternative line onto the upper mountain, and several parties pair it with the ridge path — one for the way up, one for the way down. From Virgin Lake, take the main tread down into the basin, cross or skirt the lake's south shore on logs and boulders (poles help), then work up the boulder field and heather slopes above the north shore to the glacier toe. Stay on the glacier's EAST side; the west-side ice is noticeably steeper.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Best when the glacier is snow-covered enough to bridge but firm enough to travel; midday summer slush makes it slow and sliding.
hazards: Crevasses on the Columbia Glacier — low-angle but real, especially where snow is soft
Soft, sliding midday slush in summer
Wading or log-crossing the lake outlet stream
Loose, crumbly rock on the lateral moraine and at the glacier exit
Camping is banned within half a mile of the big lake, so plan the overnight around Virgin Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the rock is the glacier's exit, and it is a specific and short one: about fifty feet of ledgy, somewhat loose third-class ground taking you off the ice onto rock, after which you traverse RIGHT toward the peak's southwest side and join the ridge line higher up. The test is the exit itself — a short ledgy step, not a long climb; if you are looking at hundreds of feet of rock rising straight off the ice, you are at the wrong point on the glacier's edge. Once on rock, the pebbly, loose 'kitty litter' ground and two narrow catwalks leading toward the summit block confirm you are on the standard line. Negative marker: if you are still gaining height on ice with cliffs above you and the summit off to the side, you have gone too far up the glacier past the exit.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's LEFT of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-early Oct
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the FAR END of the meadows, watch for an UNSIGNED path forking RIGHT (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream AND pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the SOUTHEAST and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad south-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's LEFT (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head SOUTH toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad south-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the LEFT (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a south-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road to the washout gate — closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood and still closed. Park there. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
approach_variants.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
A bergschrund at the head of the Eel that is hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
The Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions state
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus roughly 11 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS FLYPAPER PASS, AND THE TEST IS WHICH THINGS ARE ON WHICH SIDE OF IT. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between MOUNT ANDERSON on the east and ECHO ROCK (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

THE APPROACH TEST, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse ABOVE the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

SECOND TEST, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older published figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — those descriptions are old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.

approach_variants.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
approach_variants.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a TRAIL the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
hazards: Everything above the pass is the same: the 40-45 degree snow finger, the Eel Glacier crevasses and bergschrund, and loose summit rock
A long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
Arriving at the pass from the west means the shelter and the climbers' path are both below and behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage anywhere on either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE DOSEWALLIPS VARIANT ABOVE, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when MOUNT ANDERSON is on one side of the notch and ECHO ROCK on the other.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves NORTH off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
approach_variants.notes: READ THE NAME ON THIS ROUTE WITH CARE — it says West Slopes and the climb is on the NORTH side. Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 15.3-16.7 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: A loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col that has changed between seasons — treat published descriptions of it as provisional
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier with a moat at its top whose width varies year to year and by time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk, and refreezing snow in it on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
A thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Extreme remoteness — an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or a helicopter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM LOWER MARTINS PARK THERE IS ONE BROAD SNOW-AND-ROCK COULOIR AND IT RUNS SOUTH TOWARD THE PEAK. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you SOUTH — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS A NUMBER AND A DURATION: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a SADDLE ON THE NORTH RIDGE near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you DROP down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the CHRISTIE GLACIER. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a MOAT forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

WHAT WAITS AT THE COL, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
approach_variants.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the September 2024 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Road closure at Olympic Hot Springs Road adds 6.2 miles each way and may change season to season
Everything above Low Divide is the same as the Quinault variant: the Class 4 step above the col, the Christie Glacier moat, and the entry couloir
A long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE QUINAULT VARIANT ONCE YOU ARE AT LOW DIVIDE, and that shared test is a good one: from LOWER Martins Park there is ONE broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs SOUTH toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the NORTH ridge near 5,600 ft; then DOWN loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route LEAVES maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: The southeast-facing chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
A very popular and crowded trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on route
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION POINT ON THIS MOUNTAIN IS A SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, AND A SIGN IS THE BEST FOG MARKER THERE IS BECAUSE IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON VISIBILITY BEYOND ARM'S LENGTH. At that junction the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the MAINTAINED SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the LEFT one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

SECOND TEST, higher: the summer trail threads a NARROW NOTCH and then crosses WEST-FACING slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS SEASONAL RATHER THAN NAVIGATIONAL: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: Same as the upper-trailhead variant, over a longer and gentler approach
The 3,900 ft merge is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
No water on the upper route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS THE MERGE AT ABOUT 3,900 FT, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take DOWNHILL to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

THE DECISION POINT IS THE SAME SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT up the chute, the SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT. Take the left.

AND THE SAME CONFIRMATIONS ABOVE IT: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SIGNED TIMBERLINE JUNCTION AT ABOUT 4,500 FT AND THE RIGHT-HAND BRANCH OUT OF IT. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THAT THE GROUND STOPS SWITCHBACKING. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

THE TEST FOR WHETHER YOU SHOULD BE THERE AT ALL, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
approach_variants.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant ends at camp, not at climbing. The confirmation you are at Glacier Meadows rather than somewhere short of it is the washout ladder and fixed rope just below it — if you have not climbed a ladder, you are still below.

From the meadows a way trail runs about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine, a narrow exposed catwalk with loose rock underfoot, then follows the crest roughly another 0.2 mile before dropping onto the toe of the Blue Glacier. The drop onto the ice is where you rope up; nothing before it is glacier travel.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for straightforward glacier travel
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because THE TRUE SUMMIT IS NOT VISIBLE from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is EAST of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the LEFT, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.notes: THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH AND THE ROUTE'S WAYPOINT LIST DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT ONE. Published and trip-report accounts are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 2,800-3,000 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND AT LAKE OF THE ANGELS AND THE CIRQUE ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH WAY TO GO: MOUNT STONE IS ON YOUR RIGHT, ANOTHER PEAK IS ON YOUR LEFT, AND MOUNT SKOKOMISH IS STRAIGHT AHEAD. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

THE TURN IS AROUND THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE LAKE, on a way trail heading WEST to the ridge. Then take a broad gully SOUTHWEST and up toward the SADDLE JUST NORTH OF POINT 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours SOUTH and SOUTHWEST across scree, grass and rock benches around the EAST and SOUTH flanks of the peak, PASSING A LARGE TARN. The tarn is the confirmation. TURN RIGHT AND START CLIMBING WHEN YOU ARE ABOVE THE LARGE TARN — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

THIRD TEST, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around LEFT to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has THREE SUMMIT HORNS and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

EXPLICIT WARNING FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is directional: contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut WEST over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: RECORDED BECAUSE THE ROUTE'S OWN WAYPOINTS DESCRIBE THIS APPROACH, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford HUCKLEBERRY CREEK at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot ROOT AND ROCK LADDERS, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail. Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE ON THIS SIDE IS THE OPEN BASIN AND SADDLE BENEATH THE SOUTH PEAK AT ABOUT 5,500 FT, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS UNDERFOOT: THE FOOTING TURNS TO LOOSE, ROTTEN ROCK FROM THERE UP. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. THE TEST FOR THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE ROOT LADDER, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT IS SECOND: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Published and trip-report accounts put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the north-facing basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS A NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS A TURN YOU MAKE BEFORE A GATE. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward ST. PETER'S GATE — the obvious notch above the basin. JUST BEFORE THE GATE, TURN SHARPLY LEFT (SOUTH) and traverse along the BASE OF THE CLIFFS to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. SECOND TEST, at the notch: turn RIGHT and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short LOW CLASS 3 CHIMNEY to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. THIRD TEST, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a GROOVE on the LEFT side that BENDS RIGHT, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TIMING SAYS: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. FOG WARNING SPECIFIC TO THIS MOUNTAIN: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
approach_variants.baseFinding: COMING FROM THE EAST YOU ARRIVE AT ST. PETER'S GATE ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HIGH POINT OF THE TRAVERSE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT AND AN OBVIOUS ROCKY NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S SOUTHEAST RIDGE. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. FROM THE GATE THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO THE PEAK AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT CLIMBS. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go THROUGH the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the WEST ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. SO THE FOG TEST FOR THIS VARIANT IS WHICH SIDE OF THE GATE YOU END UP ON: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. ABOVE THE NOTCH THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 CHIMNEY to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a GROOVE on the LEFT that BENDS RIGHT to the true south summit.

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, rising traverse to the Taboo Glacier
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-4 to high camp, about 1-2 more to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Bergschrund or moat at the base of the couloir — fatal accident on record
Loose class 3-4 rock in the gully with parties above
Featureless traverse from Boston Basin, easy to lose in whiteout
Early-season avalanche exposure on the traverse; buried creek channels
Couloir can be entirely melted out late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at a prominent notch in the South Ridge, at the top of the east couloir that comes off the Taboo Glacier — and the couloir, not the notch, is what you are hunting for from the glacier.

Follow the Taboo up until a deep gully or couloir breaks through the rock band on your left. It is a definite break, not a weakness in a face. A bergschrund or moat guards its bottom; this crossing is the standard place parties stop, put the sharp end on, and it has been the site of a fatal accident, so it is not a formality. Early season it is snow-bridged; late season it is wide open and the couloir above it may be completely melted out to rock.

From the schrund, scramble roughly a hundred feet of loose class 3-4 up the gully to the notch. You are at the base of the route when you are standing in a notch on the ridge crest with Torment Basin dropping away on the west side and the Taboo Glacier below you to the east. If you have gained rock but there is no crest and no view down the far side, you have gone up a break in the rock band rather than the couloir.

The late-season workaround is worth knowing, because it removes the moat problem entirely: instead of crossing onto the ridge at the notch, cross the South Ridge at about 6,600 ft and gain the ridge from the Torment Basin side. Adjacent scrambling variations that avoid the snow couloir and reach the same notch are also described.

Be aware this gully is a queue on a busy weekend — parties commonly wait below the schrund for the group above to clear the loose class 3-4 rather than climb underneath them.

approach_variants.name: Torment Basin climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
A separate and much less-used way in that skips Boston Basin altogether. Drive Cascade River Road only about 20 miles — roughly a mile past the Eldorado Creek trailhead — and look for the climbers' path starting about fifty feet upstream of the bridge over the Cascade River.

It is a steep, hard climb on a boot path that is mostly easy to follow up into Torment Basin, but despite decades of traffic some sections stay genuinely brushy. It puts you on the west side of the South Ridge rather than the east.

The reason to use it is the moat: from the Torment Basin side the South Ridge can be gained at about 6,600 ft without crossing the moat at the top of the Taboo Glacier, which is the late-season crux of the standard approach. It is also the shorter drive.
approach_variants.season: midsummer once brush is passable
hazards: Brushy sections on a steep unmaintained boot path
Less-travelled approach — fewer parties, less current beta on conditions
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming from Torment Basin you meet the South Ridge from the west, so you do not arrive at the notch from below — you gain the crest at about 6,600 ft and follow it. The confirmation is the crest itself and the Taboo Glacier appearing below on the east side once you are on it. This is the same ridge the standard approach reaches at the notch above the couloir, entered lower down.

approach_variants.name: Clearwater Creek gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive to the gate before the Clearwater Creek / Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on the logging-road network west of Mosquito Lake Road. From the gate it is roughly 6-6.5 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over Clearwater Creek and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay RIGHT; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the LEFT branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right on the crest into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after Clearwater Creek near the gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRT MOUND AND CAIRN AT ABOUT MILE 5 IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER ON THIS APPROACH, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE NAVIGATION GETS HARD. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — RIGHT at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then LEFT at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

THE FIRE RING AT ABOUT MILE 6.4 IS THE SECOND MARKER, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

IN LOW CLOUD, WHICH IS NORMAL HERE, THE CLEARCUT IS THE HARDEST GROUND ON THE ROUTE AND IT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

THE ONE PIECE OF BETA THAT REPEATS IN EVERY ACCOUNT, AND IT IS THE FOG TEST FOR THE RIDGE ITSELF: STAY LEFT — CLIMBER'S LEFT — ON THE CREST. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting RIGHT leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT RANGE. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.notes:
The other documented way onto the same ridge, from the other side of the road network: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap on the ridge crest
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROAD NETWORK IS THE CRUX AND THE MOUNTAIN IS NOT. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. THE END OF RIDEABLE ROAD IS THE MARKER, and on this network it is commonly identified by a LARGE CULVERT PIPE at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot. THE CLIMBERS' PATH IS BRUSHY AND WET AND NOT HARD TO FOLLOW — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.
