ARRIVAL: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. On the crest, STAY CLIMBER'S LEFT; drifting right puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground. WHICH SISTER AM I ON? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. NORTH TWIN's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. SOUTH TWIN's west ridge is gained at an obvious NOTCH in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY ABOVE THE LAKE IS THE ROUTE AND IT IS THE WORST GROUND OF THE DAY - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the RIB THAT PARALLELS IT, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

IF THE GROUND YOU ARE CLIMBING IS PLEASANT, YOU ARE NOT IN THE RIGHT GULLY. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS ON THE RIDGE, NOT ON THE APPROACH: A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE, AND IT IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble EASTWARD along the ridge. IF YOU TOPPED OUT OF THE GULLY AND WENT LEFT TO A SUMMIT WITHIN A FEW MINUTES, YOU ARE ON THE LOWER POINT WEST OF THE SADDLE.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE TOP IS THE WALK. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.

approach_variants.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
approach_variants.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS AT THE LAKE AND THE RIDGE ABOVE IT BEGINS. The south-east ridge rises from the lake basin toward a col at about 8,000 ft - the ridge is the handrail and it should have ground falling away on both sides once you are established on it.

IF YOU FIND YOURSELF IN A CONFINED, VERY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE DROPPED OFF THE CREST INTO ONE OF THE GULLIES ON ITS FLANK. That is the other route's ground, approached from the other drainage, and it is not where this line goes.

AT THE COL, THE SUMMIT IS THE HIGH POINT ALONG THE CREST AND IT IS NOT THE FIRST BUMP. The ridge here carries several intervening high points, and a small peak stands west of the ridge saddle that is regularly mistaken for the top. THE TRUE SUMMIT IS THE EASTERN HIGH POINT; if you have gone west from a saddle and arrived quickly, you are on the wrong one.

The practical cross-check is talus. Reaching the true summit involves a tedious out-and-back over talus and large boulders rather than a quick step up from wherever you gained the crest.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROUTE IS ENTERED AT A COL, AND THERE ARE TWO COLS IN A ROW - GETTING THE ORDER RIGHT IS THE NAVIGATION. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the first glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow. Cross OVER the first col, then DESCEND the second, larger glacier to about 7,200 ft, then TRAVERSE RIGHT - eastward - across it. THE COL YOU WANT IS AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND IT SITS BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS LARGER NEIGHBOUR TO THE WEST. A BERGSCHRUND GUARDS IT and can be hard to cross late in the season, sometimes needing a short rappel to get down onto or across it. THE SCHRUND IS THE CONFIRMATION AS MUCH AS THE OBSTACLE: a col reached without one is likely the first col, not the second. THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE COL IS WHERE YOU GO NEXT: CONTOUR ON AN EASY SNOWFIELD ROUND TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE and climb a loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge. IF YOU ARE STILL ON THE NORTH OR SHADED SIDE OF THE CREST WITH THE FACE ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE NOT CONTOURED FAR ENOUGH ROUND. THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT WHICH MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON. THE SUMMIT LIES JUST UNDER A MILE EAST OF ITS BETTER-KNOWN NEIGHBOUR ALONG THE CONNECTING RIDGE. If you have topped out on the summit block immediately above the first col you crossed, you are on the neighbour, not on this peak. Keep going east. There is also a direct alternative from the col: an exposed class 3+ ridge taken straight from the saddle instead of the gully. Both finish on the same crest; the gully is the standard and the loose rock in it is the main hazard on the climb.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
approach_variants.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col
approach_variants.baseFinding:
EITHER CAMP FEEDS THE SAME LINE: TRAVERSE THE UPPER BASINS NEAR 7,000 FT TO GAIN THE FIRST GLACIER, CROSS ITS COL, DESCEND THE SECOND GLACIER TO ABOUT 7,200 FT, AND TRAVERSE EAST TO THE 7,640 FT COL BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR.

COUNT THE COLS. The first is crossed and the second is the destination, with a bergschrund on it. Standing at a col with a large icefield behind you and the summit block immediately above is the FIRST col and the neighbouring peak, not this one.

FROM THE CORRECT COL, CONTOUR ROUND ON EASY SNOW TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE AND FIND THE LOOSE GULLY. A route that climbs directly out of the col on exposed class 3+ crest is the direct variant rather than the standard, so choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

If you camped at the lake, budget the extra height gain into the morning; if you camped on the ridge, budget the wind into the night.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other. The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
approach_variants.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through Jun
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe EASIER to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THE TRAP IS THAT THERE ARE TWO SUMMITS. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

AT THE COL, CHECK WHICH TOWER YOU ARE UNDER. THIS ROUTE IS ON THE EASTERN SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE HARDER AND HIGHER OF THE PAIR. IF THE PEAK ABOVE YOU IS THE ONE YOU TRAVERSED BENEATH ON THE WAY IN, YOU ARE FACING THE WESTERN SUMMIT AND HAVE TURNED THE WRONG WAY OUT OF THE SADDLE.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE THE COL IS A LADDER OF SPECIFIC SHAPES, IN ORDER, AND IT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE RIGHT: a ramp leading RIGHT past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief DESCENT to a small flat area. THE FLAT SPOT AFTER A DOWNCLIMB IS THE CONFIRMATION - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

FROM THAT FLAT AREA, LOCATE THE CORRECT GULLY LEADING TO A HIGH NOTCH ON THE WEST RIDGE. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. IF YOU ARE UNCOILING A ROPE AT THE COL ITSELF, YOU ARE HUNDREDS OF FEET TOO LOW.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM EITHER CAMP THE ROUTE MEETS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE SADDLE BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

THE HIGH CAMP'S OWN MARKER IS THAT IT SITS ON ROCK OUTCROPS AT THE GLACIER'S EDGE at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

AT THE SADDLE, THE SUMMIT YOU WANT IS THE EASTERN ONE - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

THE CONFIRMATION SEQUENCE IS THE SAME LADDER: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short DOWNCLIMB to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: In the basin, The Scoop starts to the RIGHT of the West Face and the Tempest and to the LEFT of Rikki Tikki Tavi. The confirmation is not at the ground but three pitches up: the first three pitches, to about 5.10a, lead to LAUNCH LEDGE, the platform sitting directly below the namesake Scoop corner. If the ledge you reach after three pitches has no large corner system rising above it, you are not on The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble to the wall.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cairns mark the base of the correct gully and stop there. Leftmost is the test. From the basin, The Scoop is right of the West Face and Tempest and left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; Launch Ledge, three pitches up with the Scoop corner above it, is what confirms the line.

approach_variants.name: Road walk from the pullout to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes: From Randle, head south and follow the main forest road roughly nineteen miles, then turn off at the signed meadows turning and follow the next road under three miles before turning again onto the last one. That final road is rough and wants high clearance; follow it about two miles until the rock appears, then carry on to the large pullout where the climbers' trail is obvious. From the pullout, simply walk up the road toward the wall and onto its base. There is no cell service on the approach or at the crag.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia studded with cobbles and knobs that can pop loose without warning
Rough gravel approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service on the approach or at the crag
The formation's base wraps a long way; the toe is a specific point, not a general area
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go to the LOWEST TOE of the West Face — the point where the wall's base comes down closest to the road, rather than anywhere along its higher flanks. The start is a short PROW, and the test is bolts you can count: TWO of them, low, on the prow, within reach from the ground. Confirm from the pitches above — the first climbs a short face onto clean ramps to a ledge belay, and the second traverses across a SADDLE to a CHAIN ANCHOR, which is a distinctive shape for a second pitch and not something a neighbouring line does. Negative marker: if you are under a long face with no bolts within reach of the ground and the only protection on offer is slinging the embedded cobbles and knobs, you are on one of the older knob-slinging lines rather than this bolted one.

approach_variants.name: Around the East Face and through the Gap
approach_variants.notes: The other way onto this side of the formation, and the one to use if you are coming from routes on the far side. From the same pullout, take the climbers' trail around the EAST face of the rock — this trail traverses the whole formation — and pass through the deep gully that splits it, then drop down to the LEFT onto the West Face's base. It is longer than walking up the road but it links the two sides without returning to the car.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia with loose cobbles and knobs
The traverse round the formation is on climbers' trail with loose ground below the walls
Rough approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service anywhere on the approach or at the crag
approach_variants.baseFinding: Having dropped down and left out of the walk-through gully, keep descending along the base until you reach the LOWEST TOE of the West Face — the far low point of the wall, not the first rock you meet after the gap. The start is a short PROW carrying TWO bolts within reach of the ground. Confirm above: a short face to clean ramps and a ledge belay, then a traverse across a saddle to a chain anchor. Negative markers: if the deep walk-through gully is still behind and ABOVE you and you have not dropped down and left, you are on the flank rather than at the foot of the face; if you are looking at a long unbolted face where knobs are the only protection, you are on an older line.
